title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Endogenous Interest and Exchange Rates
text:
This example extends the endogenous-interest-rate framework to a two-country economy. International product purchases generate demand for the corresponding moneys, and the equilibrium prices of dated money services determine both interest rates and exchange rates. Positive preference weights on terminal money holdings keep all production-period interest rates finite.
Assume the following:

There are two countries, A and B. Each country has one representative firm and one representative consumer. There are six commodity types: product A, product B, labor A, labor B, money A, and money B.
The economy operates for \(n_p\geq3\) periods. Production takes place in periods \(i=1,\ldots,n_p-1\). Production in period \(i\) uses domestic labor and produces product dated \(i+1\).
Production in country \(q\in\{A,B\}\) is linear:

\[
y_q^{(i)}=\alpha_q^{(i)} l_q^{(i)},
\qquad
\alpha_q^{(i)}>0
\]

Consumer \(q\) owns \(\omega_q^{(i)}>0\) units of domestic labor in each production period and the service endowments associated with a fixed domestic money stock \(M_q>0\). Each unit of money provides one unit of service in every production period and one unit of terminal holding service.
Domestic labor purchases require domestic money. Purchases of product A require money A, whereas purchases of product B require money B. Both consumers can purchase both products and use both moneys.
Product A dated period 2 is the common numeraire:

\[
p_A^{(2)}=1
\]
All dated-commodity prices are expressed relative to this single numeraire. Throughout this section, \(q\in\{A,B\}\) denotes a country, country indices are written as subscripts, and time indices are written as parenthesized superscripts.


Let \(c_{q,j}^{(i+1)}\) denote consumer \(j\)’s consumption of country \(q\)’s product dated \(i+1\), and let \(h_{q,j}^{(n_p)}\) denote that consumer’s terminal holdings of money \(q\). Preferences are
\[
u_j=
\prod_{q\in\{A,B\}}
\left[
\left(
\prod_{i=1}^{n_p-1}
(c_{q,j}^{(i+1)})^{\beta_q^{(i)}}
\right)
(h_{q,j}^{(n_p)})^{\beta_{m,q}}
\right]^{\lambda_{qj}},
\qquad
j\in\{A,B\}
\]
where
\[
\lambda_{Aj}>0,
\qquad
\lambda_{Bj}>0,
\qquad
\lambda_{Aj}+\lambda_{Bj}=1
\]
and, for each country \(q\),
\[
\beta_q^{(1)}>\beta_q^{(2)}>\cdots>
\beta_q^{(n_p-1)}>\beta_{m,q}>0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n_p-1}\beta_q^{(i)}+\beta_{m,q}=1
\]
The parameter \(\lambda_{qj}\) is consumer \(j\)’s expenditure share allocated to country \(q\)’s consumption and terminal-money bundle. Both consumers have the same within-bundle temporal shares for a given country, but their country expenditure shares may differ.
Let \(p_q^{(t)}\), \(p_{l,q}^{(i)}\), and \(p_{m,q}^{(i)}\) denote the prices of country \(q\)’s dated product, labor, and money service, respectively. Consumer \(j\)’s income is
\[
w_j=
\sum_{i=1}^{n_p-1}p_{l,j}^{(i)}\omega_j^{(i)}
+
M_j\sum_{i=1}^{n_p}p_{m,j}^{(i)}
\]
Given the interest rates, product demand is
\[
c_{q,j}^{(i+1)}
=
\frac{\lambda_{qj}\beta_q^{(i)} w_j}
{(1+r_q^{(i)})p_q^{(i+1)}},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
The associated transaction demand for money services is
\[
h_{q,j}^{(i)}
=
\frac{\lambda_{qj}\beta_q^{(i)} w_jr_q^{(i)}}
{(1+r_q^{(i)})p_{m,q}^{(i)}}
\]
Terminal money demand is
\[
h_{q,j}^{(n_p)}
=
\frac{\lambda_{qj}\beta_{m,q} w_j}
{p_{m,q}^{(n_p)}}
\]
Define total expenditure allocated to country \(q\)’s bundle as
\[
W_q=\lambda_{qA}w_A+\lambda_{qB}w_B
\]
Aggregate demand for its product is therefore
\[
C_q^{(i+1)}
=
\sum_{j\in\{A,B\}}c_{q,j}^{(i+1)}
=
\frac{\beta_q^{(i)}W_q}
{(1+r_q^{(i)})p_q^{(i+1)}}
\]



An output level \(y_q^{(i)}\) requires labor and money services in quantities
\[
l_q^{(i)}=\frac{y_q^{(i)}}{\alpha_q^{(i)}},
\qquad
h_{q,f}^{(i)}
=
\frac{r_q^{(i)}p_{l,q}^{(i)}y_q^{(i)}}
{\alpha_q^{(i)}p_{m,q}^{(i)}}
\]
The firm’s unit revenue-expenditure balance condition is
\[
p_q^{(i+1)}
=
(1+r_q^{(i)})\frac{p_{l,q}^{(i)}}{\alpha_q^{(i)}}
\]
Labor- and product-market clearing give
\[
y_q^{(i)*}
=
\alpha_q^{(i)}\omega_q^{(i)}
=
C_q^{(i+1)*}
\]
Consequently,
\[
p_q^{(i+1)*}
=
\frac{\beta_q^{(i)}W_q^*}
{(1+r_q^{(i)*})\alpha_q^{(i)}\omega_q^{(i)}}
\]
and
\[
p_{l,q}^{(i)*}
=
\frac{\alpha_q^{(i)}p_q^{(i+1)*}}
{1+r_q^{(i)*}}
\]
money-service market clearing requires
\[
h_{q,f}^{(i)}+h_{q,A}^{(i)}+h_{q,B}^{(i)}=M_q
\]
Substitution gives
\[
M_qp_{m,q}^{(i)*}
=
\beta_q^{(i)}W_q^*
\frac{r_q^{(i)*}(r_q^{(i)*}+2)}
{(1+r_q^{(i)*})^2},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
Terminal money-market clearing gives
\[
M_qp_{m,q}^{(n_p)*}=\beta_{m,q}W_q^*
\]
Together with the interest-rate relations below, the agents’ revenue-expenditure balance conditions and the commodity-market clearing conditions define the structural equilibrium model.



The production-period price \(p_{m,q}^{(i)}\) represents the value of the service supplied by one unit of money \(q\) during period \(i\). It is distinct from the value of the money itself. The terminal price \(p_{m,q}^{(n_p)}\) represents the value of its terminal holding service.
Define the beginning-of-period value of one unit of money \(q\) as
\[
v_q^{(i)}=\sum_{s=i}^{n_p}p_{m,q}^{(s)},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p
\]
Since these are dated-commodity prices under a common numeraire, no additional discount factors are applied to this sum.
The production-period ad valorem claim rate is
\[
r_q^{(i)}=\frac{p_{m,q}^{(i)}}{v_q^{(i+1)}},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
Thus,
\[
v_q^{(i)}=(1+r_q^{(i)})v_q^{(i+1)}
\]
Normalize the total money value by expenditure:
\[
g_q^{(i)}=\frac{M_qv_q^{(i)}}{W_q}
\]
Then
\[
g_q^{(n_p)}=\beta_{m,q},
\qquad
1+r_q^{(i)}=\frac{g_q^{(i)}}{g_q^{(i+1)}}
\]
For a strictly positive interest-rate solution, money-market clearing implies
\[
(g_q^{(i)})^2-\beta_q^{(i)}g_q^{(i)}-\beta_q^{(i)}g_q^{(i+1)}=0
\]
The positive root gives the backward recursion
\[
g_q^{(i)}=
\frac{
\beta_q^{(i)}+
\sqrt{(\beta_q^{(i)})^2+4\beta_q^{(i)}g_q^{(i+1)}}
}{2},
\qquad
i=n_p-1,\ldots,1
\]
Starting from \(g_q^{(n_p)}=\beta_{m,q}\), this determines the equilibrium interest rates:
\[
r_q^{(i)*}=\frac{g_q^{(i)}}{g_q^{(i+1)}}-1
\]
The decreasing-share assumption guarantees positivity. At the terminal step, \(\beta_{m,q}<\beta_q^{(n_p-1)}\) implies
\[
g_q^{(n_p)}<g_q^{(n_p-1)}<2\beta_q^{(n_p-1)}
\]
At each preceding step, \(g_q^{(i+1)}<2\beta_q^{(i+1)}<2\beta_q^{(i)}\) implies
\[
g_q^{(i+1)}<g_q^{(i)}<2\beta_q^{(i)}
\]
Hence,
\[
g_q^{(1)}>g_q^{(2)}>\cdots>g_q^{(n_p)}>0
\]
and every production-period interest rate is finite and strictly positive.



For each production period, domestic labor income and domestic money-service income satisfy
\[
p_{l,q}^{(i)*}\omega_q^{(i)}+M_qp_{m,q}^{(i)*}
=
\beta_q^{(i)}W_q^*
\]
Adding terminal money income yields
\[
w_q^*=W_q^*
\]
The equilibrium income vector therefore satisfies
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
w_A^*\\
w_B^*
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\lambda_{AA}&\lambda_{AB}\\
\lambda_{BA}&\lambda_{BB}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
w_A^*\\
w_B^*
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Since each column of the expenditure-share matrix sums to one,
\[
\frac{w_A^*}{w_B^*}
=
\frac{\lambda_{AB}}{\lambda_{BA}}
\]
The numeraire condition determines the income scale:
\[
w_A^*
=
\frac{
(1+r_A^{(1)*})\alpha_A^{(1)}\omega_A^{(1)}
}{
\beta_A^{(1)}
}
\]
Let \(e_{AB}^{(i)}\) denote the number of units of money B equivalent in value to one unit of money A at the beginning of period \(i\). Then
\[
e_{AB}^{(i)*}=\frac{v_A^{(i)*}}{v_B^{(i)*}}
\]
Using \(v_q^{(i)*}=w_q^*g_q^{(i)}/M_q\) gives
\[
e_{AB}^{(i)*}
=
\frac{M_B}{M_A}
\frac{\lambda_{AB}}{\lambda_{BA}}
\frac{g_A^{(i)}}{g_B^{(i)}},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p
\]
Thus, the exchange rate depends on relative money stocks, the equilibrium income ratio, and the normalized remaining values of the two moneys. It is generally different from the ratio of their current money-service prices.
Moreover,
\[
\frac{e_{AB}^{(i+1)*}}{e_{AB}^{(i)*}}
=
\frac{1+r_B^{(i)*}}{1+r_A^{(i)*}},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
This relation follows directly from the money-value and claim-rate definitions. Interpreting these rates as returns on separately traded bonds would require an additional asset-market specification.

title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Endogenous Interest and Exchange Rates
text:
Numerical Example
Consider three periods, with production in periods 1 and 2 and terminal money holdings in period 3. Let
\[
\alpha_A^{(i)}=\alpha_B^{(i)}=1,
\qquad
\omega_A^{(i)}=\omega_B^{(i)}=100,
\qquad
i=1,2
\]
and
\[
M_A=M_B=1
\]
The country expenditure-share matrix, with rows representing country bundles and columns representing consumers, is
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\lambda_{AA}&\lambda_{AB}\\
\lambda_{BA}&\lambda_{BB}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac34&\frac14\\
\frac14&\frac34
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The temporal shares are
\[
(\beta_A^{(1)},\beta_A^{(2)},\beta_{m,A})
=
\left(\frac8{15},\frac4{15},\frac15\right)
\]
and
\[
(\beta_B^{(1)},\beta_B^{(2)},\beta_{m,B})
=
\left(\frac{27}{40},\frac9{40},\frac1{10}\right)
\]
Both share sequences satisfy the strict decreasing-share assumption.
The backward recursion gives
\[
(g_A^{(1)},g_A^{(2)},g_A^{(3)})
=
\left(\frac45,\frac25,\frac15\right)
\]
and
\[
(g_B^{(1)},g_B^{(2)},g_B^{(3)})
=
\left(\frac9{10},\frac3{10},\frac1{10}\right)
\]
Consequently,
\[
r_A^{(1)*}=r_A^{(2)*}=1,
\qquad
r_B^{(1)*}=r_B^{(2)*}=2
\]
With \(p_A^{(2)}=1\), equilibrium incomes are
\[
w_A^*=w_B^*=375
\]

Each country produces 100 units in each production period:
\[
y_A^{(1)*}=y_A^{(2)*}=y_B^{(1)*}=y_B^{(2)*}=100
\]
For each consumption period \(t=2,3\), the consumption matrix is
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
c_{A,A}^{(t)*}&c_{A,B}^{(t)*}\\
c_{B,A}^{(t)*}&c_{B,B}^{(t)*}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
75&25\\
25&75
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Thus, each country consumes 75 units of its own product and imports 25 units of the other country’s product.
In each production period, the money-A service allocation is
\[
(h_{A,f}^{(i)*},h_{A,A}^{(i)*},h_{A,B}^{(i)*})
=
\left(\frac13,\frac12,\frac16\right)
\]
The money-B service allocation is
\[
(h_{B,f}^{(i)*},h_{B,A}^{(i)*},h_{B,B}^{(i)*})
=
\left(\frac14,\frac3{16},\frac9{16}\right)
\]
Each allocation sums to the corresponding money stock of one. Terminal money holdings are
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
h_{A,A}^{(3)*}&h_{A,B}^{(3)*}\\
h_{B,A}^{(3)*}&h_{B,B}^{(3)*}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac34&\frac14\\
\frac14&\frac34
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The money-value paths are
\[
(v_A^{(1)*},v_A^{(2)*},v_A^{(3)*})
=
(300,150,75)
\]
and
\[
(v_B^{(1)*},v_B^{(2)*},v_B^{(3)*})
=
\left(\frac{675}{2},\frac{225}{2},\frac{75}{2}\right)
\]
Therefore, the equilibrium exchange-rate path is
\[
(e_{AB}^{(1)*},e_{AB}^{(2)*},e_{AB}^{(3)*})
=
\left(\frac89,\frac43,2\right)
\]
It satisfies
\[
\frac{e_{AB}^{(2)*}}{e_{AB}^{(1)*}}
=
\frac{e_{AB}^{(3)*}}{e_{AB}^{(2)*}}
=
\frac32
=
\frac{1+2}{1+1}
\]

title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Production and Endogenous Interest Rates
text:
In structural equilibrium models, money is usually treated as an ad valorem claim, and the interest rate is usually treated as an ad valorem claim rate (Li, 2019, chap. 7). This example considers a finite-horizon intertemporal equilibrium with production and endogenous interest rates. There are three types of dated commodities—product, labor, and money—and two types of economic agents—firm and consumer.
Assume the following:

The economy operates for \(n_p\geq3\) periods, indexed by \(1,\ldots,n_p\). Production takes place in periods \(i=1,\ldots,n_p-1\). Production in period \(i\) produces product \(i+1\), which is available in period \(i+1\). Accordingly, the dated products are product \(2,\ldots,n_p\), while the dated labor and money commodities are labor \(1,\ldots,n_p-1\) and money \(1,\ldots,n_p-1\). There is no product 1 commodity in the model; the first product generated by production is product 2. Thus, there are \(3(n_p-1)\) dated commodities. There is one firm activity in each of the first \(n_p-1\) periods and one consumer. Product 2 is the numeraire.
In production period \(i\), the firm uses labor \(l^{(i)}\) to produce product \(i+1\) according to

\[
y^{(i)}=\alpha^{(i)} l^{(i)},
\qquad
\alpha^{(i)}>0
\]
Let \(y^{(i)}\) also denote the firm’s activity level, measured by output. Thus, producing \(y^{(i)}\) units of product \(i+1\) requires \(y^{(i)}/\alpha^{(i)}\) units of labor \(i\). Before production, the firm presells product \(i+1\) and uses money \(i\) to purchase labor \(i\).

The consumer has the intertemporal Cobb–Douglas utility function

\[
u=\prod_{i=1}^{n_p-1}\left(c^{(i+1)}\right)^{\beta^{(i)}}
\]
where \(c^{(i+1)}\) denotes consumption of product \(i+1\), produced in period \(i\). The expenditure shares are strictly decreasing over production periods,
\[
\beta^{(1)}>\beta^{(2)}>\cdots>\beta^{(n_p-1)}>0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n_p-1}\beta^{(i)}=1
\]
The consumer is endowed with \(\omega^{(i)}>0\) units of labor \(i\), \(i=1,\ldots,n_p-1\). The decreasing-share assumption will ensure strictly positive equilibrium interest rates in all nonterminal production periods. 4. The consumer is endowed with one unit of money in each production period \(i=1,\ldots,n_p-1\). Let \(p_m^{(i)}\) denote the price of money \(i\). We restrict attention to equilibria with strictly positive nonterminal interest rates,
\[
r^{(i)}>0,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
while the terminal condition is
\[
r^{(n_p-1)}=+\infty
\]
For the terminal production period, define the finite interest-inclusive product price
\[
\tilde p^{(n_p)}
:=
\lim_{r^{(n_p-1)}\rightarrow+\infty}
(1+r^{(n_p-1)})p^{(n_p)}
\]
This variable allows the terminal demands to be written directly without introducing an infinite interest rate into the equilibrium system.
For the four-period case, \(n_p=4\), there are three production periods. Let
\[
\mathbf p
=
\left(
1,p^{(3)},p^{(4)},
p_l^{(1)},p_l^{(2)},p_l^{(3)},
p_m^{(1)},p_m^{(2)},p_m^{(3)}
\right)^\top
\]
let \(\mathbf y=(y^{(1)},y^{(2)},y^{(3)})^\top\) denote firm activity levels, and let \(w\) denote consumer income. The consumer’s income is the value of the labor and money endowments,
\[
w
=
\sum_{i=1}^3p_l^{(i)}\omega^{(i)}
+
\sum_{i=1}^3p_m^{(i)}
\]
With rows representing product 2–4, labor 1–3, and money 1–3, and columns representing the three firms and the consumer, respectively, the demand matrix is
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\mathbf y,w,r^{(1)},r^{(2)},\tilde p^{(4)})
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta^{(1)}w}{1+r^{(1)}}\\[6pt]
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta^{(2)}w}{(1+r^{(2)})p^{(3)}}\\[6pt]
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta^{(3)}w}{\tilde p^{(4)}}\\[6pt]
\dfrac{y^{(1)}}{\alpha^{(1)}}&0&0&0\\[6pt]
0&\dfrac{y^{(2)}}{\alpha^{(2)}}&0&0\\[6pt]
0&0&\dfrac{y^{(3)}}{\alpha^{(3)}}&0\\[6pt]
\dfrac{r^{(1)}p_l^{(1)}y^{(1)}}{\alpha^{(1)}p_m^{(1)}}&0&0&
\dfrac{\beta^{(1)}wr^{(1)}}{(1+r^{(1)})p_m^{(1)}}\\[8pt]
0&\dfrac{r^{(2)}p_l^{(2)}y^{(2)}}{\alpha^{(2)}p_m^{(2)}}&0&
\dfrac{\beta^{(2)}wr^{(2)}}{(1+r^{(2)})p_m^{(2)}}\\[8pt]
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta^{(3)}w}{p_m^{(3)}}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and the supply matrix is
\[
\mathbf S(\mathbf y)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y^{(1)}&0&0&0\\
0&y^{(2)}&0&0\\
0&0&y^{(3)}&0\\
0&0&0&\omega^{(1)}\\
0&0&0&\omega^{(2)}\\
0&0&0&\omega^{(3)}\\
0&0&0&1\\
0&0&0&1\\
0&0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The third firm’s zero money demand is a terminal-limit result rather than an additional assumption. As the terminal interest rate tends to infinity, the terminal product price and the third-period labor price both tend to zero in a way that makes the firm’s money demand vanish. Under the same terminal-limit treatment, the consumer’s terminal-period product and money demands are written directly in terms of \(\tilde p^{(4)}\) and \(p_m^{(3)}\).
For each nonterminal production period, labor- and product-market clearing, together with the firm’s revenue-expenditure balance condition, determine the firm’s equilibrium money demand. Combining the firm’s and consumer’s money demands with money-market clearing gives
\[
p_m^{(i)*}
=
\beta^{(i)}w^*
\frac{
r^{(i)*}(r^{(i)*}+2)
}{
(1+r^{(i)*})^2
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
Under the terminal condition, the terminal firm’s money demand vanishes, while the consumer holds the entire unit of terminal money. Hence,
\[
p_m^{(n_p-1)*}
=
\beta^{(n_p-1)}w^*
\]
These money-price relations provide the basis for deriving the backward recursion for the endogenous equilibrium interest rates.

section: Analytical Solution for the Endogenous Interest Rates
text:
Analytical Solution for the Endogenous Interest Rates
The endogenous interest rates are determined by the equilibrium values of dated money. Define the tail value of money prices by
\[
v^{(i)}
:=
\sum_{j=i}^{n_p-1}p_m^{(j)*}
\]
For each nonterminal period, the ad valorem claim-rate relation is
\[
r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{p_m^{(i)*}}{v^{(i+1)}},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
Since
\[
v^{(i)}=p_m^{(i)*}+v^{(i+1)}
\]
we have
\[
1+r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{v^{(i)}}{v^{(i+1)}}
\]
Normalize the tail value by consumer income:
\[
g^{(i)}
:=
\frac{v^{(i)}}{w^*}
\]
The terminal value is
\[
g^{(n_p-1)}=\beta^{(n_p-1)}
\]
and
\[
1+r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}
\]
Using
\[
\frac{p_m^{(i)*}}{w^*}
=
r^{(i)*}g^{(i+1)}
\]
together with the money-market expression gives
\[
\left(g^{(i)}\right)^2-\beta^{(i)} g^{(i)}-\beta^{(i)} g^{(i+1)}=0
\]
Thus, the positive root yields the backward recursion
\[
g^{(i)}
=
\frac{
\beta^{(i)}+
\sqrt{
\left(\beta^{(i)}\right)^2+4\beta^{(i)} g^{(i+1)}
}
}{2},
\qquad
i=n_p-2,\ldots,1
\]
with
\[
g^{(n_p-1)}=\beta^{(n_p-1)}
\]
Once the sequence \(g^{(i)}\) is obtained, the nonterminal equilibrium interest rates follow from
\[
r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}-1,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
The decreasing-share assumption guarantees that these interest rates are strictly positive. To see this, note first that
\[
g^{(n_p-1)}=\beta^{(n_p-1)}<2\beta^{(n_p-1)}
\]
Suppose \(g^{(i+1)}<2\beta^{(i+1)}\). Since \(\beta^{(i)}>\beta^{(i+1)}\),
\[
g^{(i+1)}<2\beta^{(i)}
\]
Using
\[
\left(g^{(i)}\right)^2-\beta^{(i)} g^{(i)}-\beta^{(i)} g^{(i+1)}=0
\]
and evaluating the left-hand side at \(g^{(i+1)}\) and \(2\beta^{(i)}\) shows that the positive root satisfies
\[
g^{(i+1)}<g^{(i)}<2\beta^{(i)}
\]
This establishes the induction step. Proceeding backward therefore gives
\[
g^{(1)}>g^{(2)}>\cdots>g^{(n_p-1)}>0
\]
and hence
\[
r^{(i)*}>0,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
Thus, for any finite \(n_p\), the backward recursion directly determines the strictly positive nonterminal equilibrium interest rates under the maintained assumption \(\beta^{(1)}>\beta^{(2)}>\cdots>\beta^{(n_p-1)}>0\). The productivity parameters \(\alpha^{(i)}\) and labor endowments \(\omega^{(i)}\) affect equilibrium quantities and prices but do not enter the interest-rate recursion.

Common Nonterminal Interest Rate
A useful special case imposes a common nonterminal equilibrium interest rate,
\[
r^{(i)*}=r>0,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
Then
\[
g^{(i)}=(1+r)g^{(i+1)}
\]
and the share parameters satisfy
\[
\beta^{(i)}
=
\beta^{(n_p-1)}
\frac{
(1+r)^{n_p-i}
}{
r+2
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
Together with \(\sum_{i=1}^{n_p-1}\beta^{(i)}=1\), this determines the complete sequence of shares. Under the maintained decreasing-share assumption, the common-rate specification must also satisfy
\[
\beta^{(n_p-2)}>\beta^{(n_p-1)}
\]
which, using the expression above, is equivalent to
\[
\frac{(1+r)^2}{r+2}>1
\]
or
\[
r>\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}
\]
For earlier periods, \(\beta^{(i)}/\beta^{(i+1)}=1+r>1\), so this terminal-adjacent condition is sufficient for the entire sequence to be strictly decreasing. In particular, when \(r=1\),
\[
\beta^{(i)}
=
\frac{
2^{n_p-i}
}{
2^{n_p}-1
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
and
\[
\beta^{(n_p-1)}
=
\frac{3}{2^{n_p}-1}
\]
which gives
\[

\]

title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Production and Endogenous Interest Rates
text:
Infinite-Horizon Equilibrium
Consider an infinite-horizon version of the model, with production periods indexed by \(i=1,2,\ldots\). Production in period \(i\) uses labor \(i\) to produce product \(i+1\). There is no terminal production period and hence no terminal infinite-interest-rate condition.
Assume the following:

The consumer has geometric expenditure shares

\[
\beta^{(i)}=(1-\rho)\rho^{i-1},
\qquad
0<\rho<1,
\qquad
i=1,2,\ldots
\]
so that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\beta^{(i)}=1
\]

Productivity and labor endowment are constant over time:

\[
\alpha^{(i)}=\alpha>0,
\qquad
\omega^{(i)}=\omega>0
\]

The consumer is endowed with one unit of money in each production period. Product 2 is the numeraire.

We seek an equilibrium with finite consumer income \(w^*>0\) and summable dated-money prices. Define
\[
v^{(i)}=\sum_{j=i}^{\infty}p_m^{(j)*},
\qquad
g^{(i)}=\frac{v^{(i)}}{w^*}
\]
The ad valorem claim-rate relation implies
\[
r^{(i)*}=\frac{p_m^{(i)*}}{v^{(i+1)}},
\qquad
1+r^{(i)*}=\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}
\]
As in the finite-horizon model, money-market clearing gives
\[
\frac{p_m^{(i)*}}{w^*}
=
\beta^{(i)}
\frac{r^{(i)*}(r^{(i)*}+2)}{(1+r^{(i)*})^2}
\]
For strictly positive interest rates, these relations yield
\[
\left(g^{(i)}\right)^2-\beta^{(i)} g^{(i)}-\beta^{(i)} g^{(i+1)}=0
\]
Since \(\beta^{(i+1)}=\rho\beta^{(i)}\), a proportional solution \(g^{(i)}=C\beta^{(i)}\) satisfies
\[
C=1+\rho
\]
Thus,
\[
g^{(i)}=(1+\rho)\beta^{(i)}
\]
and the equilibrium interest rate is constant:
\[
r^{(i)*}=\frac1\rho-1>0,
\qquad
i=1,2,\ldots
\]
Equivalently, writing \(r=1/\rho-1\), the expenditure shares are
\[
\beta^{(i)}=\frac{r}{(1+r)^i}
\]
The corresponding dated-money prices satisfy
\[
p_m^{(i)*}
=
w^*(g^{(i)}-g^{(i+1)})
=
w^*(1-\rho^2)\beta^{(i)}
\]
These prices are positive and summable. Moreover,
\[
\sum_{j=i}^{\infty}p_m^{(j)*}
=
w^*(1+\rho)\beta^{(i)}
=
w^*g^{(i)}
\]
so the proposed sequence is consistent with the definition of the tail value, and \(v^{(i)}\rightarrow0\) as \(i\rightarrow\infty\).
Labor- and product-market clearing give constant equilibrium output and consumption:
\[
y^{(i)*}=c^{(i+1)*}=\alpha\omega
\]
Taking product 2 as the numeraire yields
\[
w^*=\frac{\alpha\omega}{\rho(1-\rho)}
\]
The equilibrium commodity prices are
\[
p^{(i+1)*}=\rho^{i-1},
\qquad
p_l^{(i)*}=\alpha\rho^i,
\qquad
p_m^{(i)*}
=
\frac{1-\rho^2}{\rho}\alpha\omega\rho^{i-1}
\]
They satisfy the consumer-income identity
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_l^{(i)*}\omega
+
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_m^{(i)*}
=
\frac{\alpha\omega}{\rho(1-\rho)}
=
w^*
\]
The equilibrium money holdings are also constant over time:
\[
h_f^{(i)*}=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho},
\qquad
h_c^{(i)*}=\frac1{1+\rho}
\]
Thus, every dated money market clears. The infinite-horizon equilibrium has constant output, consumption, and money holdings, a constant interest rate determined by \(\rho\), and geometrically declining dated-commodity prices.

section: Steady State: A \(3\times2\) Equality-Form Wide-Sense Structural Equilibrium Model
text:
Steady State: A \(3\times2\) Equality-Form Wide-Sense Structural Equilibrium Model
The infinite-horizon steady state can be represented by a finite-dimensional equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model.
Assume the following:

There are three commodity types: product, labor, and money; and two economic-agent types: firm and consumer. Product is the numeraire.
The consumer supplies \(\omega>0\) units of labor and one unit of money, and consumes only product.
The firm uses labor to produce product according to

\[
y=\alpha l,
\qquad
\alpha>0
\]

Let \(\rho\in(0,1)\) denote the intertemporal discount factor. The steady-state interest rate is

\[
r=\frac1{\rho}-1
\]
Let
\[
\mathbf p=(1,p_l,p_m)^\top
\]
where \(p_l\) and \(p_m\) are the prices of labor and money, respectively. The prices of money represent the interest on a unit of money. For a given output level \(y\), labor demand is
\[
l=\frac{y}{\alpha}
\]
Money is required for labor purchases by the firm and product purchases by the consumer. Accordingly, the demand and supply matrices are
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0
&
c
\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\frac{y}{\alpha}
&
0
\\[10pt]
\displaystyle\frac{rp_l}{p_m}\frac{y}{\alpha}
&
\displaystyle\frac{rc}{p_m}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf S(y)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y&0\\
0&\omega\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
where the first and second columns correspond to the firm and consumer, respectively.
The steady-state equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model is
\[
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)
=
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf S(y)
\]
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)\mathbf 1
=
\mathbf S(y)\mathbf 1
\]
Solving the model gives
\[
l^*=\omega,
\qquad
y^*=c^*=\alpha\omega
\]
and
\[
p_l^*
=
\rho\alpha
\]
\[
p_m^*
=
\frac{1-\rho^2}{\rho}\alpha\omega
\]
The corresponding equilibrium money holdings are
\[
h_f^*
=
\frac{\rho}{1+\rho},
\qquad
h_c^*
=
\frac1{1+\rho}
\]
so that
\[
h_f^*+h_c^*=1
\]

title: Production OLG Equilibrium in Timeline Form
text:
Consider a finite-horizon overlapping-generations economy with production, closely related to the classical production OLG model of Diamond (1965). The model is represented in timeline form using dated commodities.
Assume the following:

The economy contains two commodity types, product and labor, and two economic-agent types, firms and consumers. There are \(n_g\) consumer generations and \(n_p=n_g+2\) periods. Hence there are \(n_p\) dated products and \(n_p-1\) dated labor commodities.
Consumer generation \(g\) lives for three periods and consumes products in periods \(g\), \(g+1\), and \(g+2\). Its Cobb–Douglas utility function is

\[
u_g
=
\left(c_g^{(g)}\right)^{\beta_1}
\left(c_g^{(g+1)}\right)^{\beta_2}
\left(c_g^{(g+2)}\right)^{\beta_3}
\]
where \(\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3=1\).
A normal generation supplies \(\omega_1\) units of labor in the first period of its life and \(\omega_2\) units in the second period, while \(\omega_3=0\). The first generation additionally owns \(y_1\) units of the initial product. Later generations own labor only.

Firm \(t\) uses the product and labor available in period \(t\) to produce the product supplied in period \(t+1\). Let \(k^{(t)}\) and \(x^{(t)}\) denote its product and labor inputs. Its Cobb–Douglas production function is

\[
y^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha
\left(k^{(t)}\right)^{\beta_f}
\left(x^{(t)}\right)^{1-\beta_f}
\] The product input \(k^{(t)}\) can be interpreted as the capital used in period \(t\).

Let \(\varGamma_l\) denote the population growth factor and \(\varGamma_p\) the steady-state growth factor of dated product prices. The total labor supply available to a firm in a stationary demographic configuration is

\[
l
=
\omega_1
+
\frac{\omega_2}{\varGamma_l}
+
\frac{\omega_3}{\varGamma_l^2}
\]
For a consumer born in period \(t\), lifetime labor income measured relative to the labor price in period \(t\) is
\[
w
=
\omega_1
+
\omega_2\varGamma_p
+
\omega_3\varGamma_p^2
\]
The steady-state equilibrium therefore satisfies
\[
\frac{
\left(1-\beta_f\varGamma_p\varGamma_l\right)l
}{
(1-\beta_f)\varGamma_p\varGamma_l
}
=
w
\left(
\beta_1
+
\frac{\beta_2}{\varGamma_p\varGamma_l}
+
\frac{\beta_3}
{\varGamma_p^2\varGamma_l^2}
\right)
\]
which determines the possible steady-state values of \(\varGamma_p\).

Given any positive solution \(\varGamma_p\) of the steady-state equation, steady-state output is

\[
y
=
\alpha^{\frac{1}{1-\beta_f}}
\left(
\beta_f\varGamma_p
\right)^{\frac{\beta_f}{1-\beta_f}}
l
\]
A useful property of the steady-state equation is that
\[
\varGamma_{p,h}
=
\frac{1}{\varGamma_l}
\]
is always a solution. Under this value, \(w=l\) and the expenditure-share term on the right-hand side sums to one. The corresponding steady-state output is
\[
y_h
=
\alpha^{\frac{1}{1-\beta_f}}
\left(
\frac{\beta_f}{\varGamma_l}
\right)^{\frac{\beta_f}{1-\beta_f}}
l
\]
Under \(\omega_1>0\), \(\beta_3>0\), and \(0<\beta_f<1\), the steady-state equation generically has at least one additional positive solution besides \(\varGamma_{p,h}=1/\varGamma_l\). Hence, except for knife-edge parameter values at which positive roots coincide, the model has multiple positive steady-state equilibria.

title: Production OLG Equilibrium in Timeline Form
text:
Numerical Example
For the numerical example, let
\[
n_g=50,
\qquad
\varGamma_l=1,
\qquad
\alpha=2,
\qquad
\beta_f=0.2
\]
\[
(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)
=
(0.1,0.1,0.8),
\qquad
(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)
=
(50,50,0)
\]
and let the first generation own \(y_1=8\) units of the initial product.
For these parameters, \(l=100\), and the steady-state equation can be reduced to
\[
(\varGamma_p-1)
\left(
\varGamma_p^2+8\varGamma_p-8
\right)
=
0
\]
It therefore has two positive solutions. The first is the general steady-state solution
\[
\varGamma_{p,h}=1
\]
with corresponding output
\[
y_h
\approx159.1
\]
The second positive solution is
\[
\varGamma_{p,l}
=
-4+2\sqrt6
\approx0.8990
\]
with corresponding output
\[
y_l
\approx154.9
\]
Thus, for the numerical parameterization, the model has two positive steady-state equilibria. The computed finite-horizon path converges in its interior to the lower-output steady state associated with \(\varGamma_{p,l}\).
The GEMB implementation is given in Listing 1.
The model contains 50 consumer generations and 51 firms. Although the beginning and end of the finite timeline are affected by the initial and terminal boundary conditions, the middle of the computed path converges essentially exactly to the lower-output analytical steady state.



Listing 1: A \(2\times2\) Production OLG Timeline Model


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling
using Plots

ng = 50
np = ng + 2

alpha = 2.0
beta_firm = 0.2
beta_consumer = [0.1, 0.1, 0.8]

population_growth = 0.0
labor_first = [50.0, 50.0, 0.0]
initial_product = 8.0

product(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:product; period=t)
labor(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=1:np,),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-100,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-100,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=labor(1),
)

for t in 1:(np - 1)
    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        GEMB.CESSpec(
            [beta_firm, 1 - beta_firm];
            es=1.0,
            alpha=alpha,
        );
        outputs=product(t + 1),
        demands=[product(t), labor(t)],
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("firm_$t"),
    )
end

for g in 1:ng
    scale = (1 + population_growth)^(g - 1)

    consumer_demands = [
        product(g),
        product(g + 1),
        product(g + 2),
    ]

    consumer_endowments = [
        labor(g),
        labor(g + 1),
    ]

    consumer_endowment_quantities = labor_first[1:2] .* scale

    if g == 1
        consumer_endowments = vcat(
            [product(1)],
            consumer_endowments,
        )
        consumer_endowment_quantities = vcat(
            [initial_product],
            consumer_endowment_quantities,
        )
    end

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        GEMB.CESSpec(
            beta_consumer;
            es=1.0,
            alpha=1.0,
        );
        demands=consumer_demands,
        endowments=consumer_endowments,
        endowment_quantities=consumer_endowment_quantities,
        name=Symbol("consumer_$g"),
    )
end

gamma_p = -4.0 + 2.0 * sqrt(6.0)

steady_labor =
    labor_first[1] +
    labor_first[2] / (1 + population_growth)

steady_output =
    alpha^(1 / (1 - beta_firm)) *
    (beta_firm * gamma_p)^(beta_firm / (1 - beta_firm)) *
    steady_labor

p0 = ones(2 * np - 1)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

firm_output = [
    result.agent_variable_values[t][1]
    for t in 1:(np - 1)
]

prices = result.prices
product_prices = prices[1:np]
labor_prices = prices[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)]

mid = div(np - 1, 2)
window = max(1, mid - 2):min(np - 1, mid + 2)

println()
println("Finite-horizon OLG production timeline")
println("--------------------------------------")
println("Solved: ", result.solved)
println("Generations: ", ng)
println("Periods: ", np)
println("Steady-state price-growth factor: ", gamma_p)
println("Steady-state output: ", steady_output)

println()
println("Firm output around the middle of the timeline:")
for t in window
    println("firm_", t, ": ", firm_output[t])
end

println()
println("Last seven firm outputs:")
for t in max(1, np - 7):(np - 1)
    println("firm_", t, ": ", firm_output[t])
end

println()
println("Middle price-growth factors:")
println(
    "product_", mid + 1, " / product_", mid, ": ",
    product_prices[mid + 1] / product_prices[mid],
)
println(
    "labor_", mid + 1, " / labor_", mid, ":     ",
    labor_prices[mid + 1] / labor_prices[mid],
)

output_plot = plot(
    1:length(firm_output),
    firm_output;
    xlabel="Period",
    ylabel="Output",
    label="Output",
    legend=:bottomright,
    marker=:circle,
    grid=true,
    gridalpha=1.0,
)

hline!(
    output_plot,
    [steady_output];
    label="Steady-state output",
    linestyle=:dash,

title: Production Externality
text:
This example, adapted from the numerical example in Wiesmeth (2012, p. 64), illustrates how a production externality can be represented through a negatively priced commodity and how a non-degree-one production function can be transformed into a degree-one homogeneous production function by introducing a scale claim.
Assume the following:

There are five commodities: product 1, product 2, pollution, labor, and a scale claim; and there are two firms and one consumer. Product 2 is the numeraire.
Firm 1 uses labor to produce product 1. One unit of labor produces \(\alpha_1\) units of product 1 and simultaneously generates \(\alpha_1\) units of pollution.
Firm 2 uses pollution and labor to produce product 2. Let \(x_3\) and \(x_4\) denote its pollution and labor inputs. Its production function is

\[
f(x_3,x_4)
=
\frac{\alpha_2x_4}{1+\theta x_3},
\qquad
\alpha_2,\theta>0
\]

Firm 2 follows the marginal pricing rule (see Bonnisseau, Cornet and Czarnecki, 2007).
The consumer has Cobb–Douglas preferences

\[
u(x_1,x_2)
=
x_1^\beta x_2^{1-\beta},
\qquad
0<\beta<1
\]
and is endowed with \(\omega\) units of labor and one unit of the scale claim.
The production function of firm 2 is not homogeneous of degree one. Introduce a scale-claim input \(c_s>0\) and define
\[
g(x_3,x_4,c_s)
:=
c_s
f\left(
\frac{x_3}{c_s},
\frac{x_4}{c_s}
\right)
=
\frac{\alpha_2c_sx_4}
{c_s+\theta x_3}
\]
The function \(g\) is homogeneous of degree one and satisfies
\[
g(x_3,x_4,1)=f(x_3,x_4)
\]
Let the price vector be
\[
\mathbf p
=
(p_1,1,p_3,p_4,p_5)^\top
\]
where \(p_3<0\) is the price of pollution.
Let \(y_2\) denote the output of firm 2. Under the marginal pricing rule,
\[
p_3
=
-\frac{\theta\alpha_2c_sx_4}
{(c_s+\theta x_3)^2},
\qquad
p_4
=
\frac{\alpha_2c_s}
{c_s+\theta x_3},
\qquad
p_5
=
\frac{\theta\alpha_2x_3x_4}
{(c_s+\theta x_3)^2}
\]
Together with
\[
y_2
=
\frac{\alpha_2c_sx_4}
{c_s+\theta x_3}
\]
these conditions give firm 2’s conditional demands:
\[
x_3
=
-\frac{\alpha_2-p_4}
{\alpha_2p_3}y_2,
\qquad
x_4
=
\frac{y_2}{p_4},
\qquad
c_s
=
-\frac{\theta p_4}
{\alpha_2p_3}y_2
\]
Thus, after degree-one homogenization, firm 2’s demand bundle has the form
\[
\mathbf d_2(\mathbf p,y_2)
=
y_2\mathbf a_2(\mathbf p)
\]
where the unit demand bundle is determined by commodity prices.
Let \(\ell_1\) denote the labor input of firm 1 and let \(w\) denote consumer income. With rows representing product 1, product 2, pollution, labor, and the scale claim, and columns representing firm 1, firm 2, and the consumer, respectively, the demand matrix is
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\ell_1,y_2,w)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0
&
0
&
\dfrac{\beta w}{p_1}
\\
0
&
0
&
(1-\beta)w
\\
0
&
-\dfrac{\alpha_2-p_4}{\alpha_2p_3}y_2
&
0
\\
\ell_1
&
\dfrac{y_2}{p_4}
&
0
\\
0
&
-\dfrac{\theta p_4}{\alpha_2p_3}y_2
&
0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and the supply matrix is
\[
\mathbf S(\ell_1,y_2)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\alpha_1\ell_1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & y_2 & 0\\
\alpha_1\ell_1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & \omega\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The equilibrium can therefore be written directly as the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model
\[
\mathbf p^\top
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\ell_1,y_2,w)
=
\mathbf p^\top
\mathbf S(\ell_1,y_2)
\] \[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\ell_1,y_2,w)\mathbf 1
=
\mathbf S(\ell_1,y_2)\mathbf 1
\]
Define
\[
\xi
:=
\theta\alpha_1\omega
\]
and
\[
\lambda
:=
\frac{
\xi(2\beta-1)-1+
\sqrt{
[1-\xi(2\beta-1)]^2+4\beta^2\xi
}
}{
2\beta\xi
}
\]
The equilibrium labor allocation is
\[
\mathbf l^*
=
\left(
\lambda\omega,
(1-\lambda)\omega
\right)^\top
\]
The equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
\left(
\frac{\alpha_2(1+\xi)}
{\alpha_1(1+\xi\lambda)^2},
1,
-\frac{\theta\alpha_2(1-\lambda)\omega}
{(1+\xi\lambda)^2},
\frac{\alpha_2}
{1+\xi\lambda},
\frac{\theta\alpha_1\alpha_2\lambda(1-\lambda)\omega^2}
{(1+\xi\lambda)^2}
\right)^\top
\]
and the consumer’s equilibrium income is
\[
w^*
=
\frac{\alpha_2(1-\lambda)\omega}
{(1-\beta)(1+\xi\lambda)}
\]
For
\[
\alpha_1=2.5,
\qquad
\alpha_2=50,
\qquad
\theta=1,
\qquad
\omega=10,
\qquad
\beta=0.5
\]
which correspond to the parameter values in Wiesmeth (2012, p. 64), the equilibrium labor allocation is
\[
\mathbf l^*
=
\left(
\frac{2(\sqrt{26}-1)}5,
\frac{2(26-\sqrt{26})}5
\right)^\top
\approx
(1.6396,8.3604)^\top
\]
The equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*
\approx
(20.0000,\ 1.0000,\ -16.0777,\ 9.8058,\ 65.9027)^\top
\]
and the consumer’s income is
\[
w^*
\approx163.9608
\]
The corresponding pollution input and scale-claim input of firm 2 are
\[
x_3^*
=
\alpha_1\ell_1^*
\approx4.0990,
\qquad
c_s^*=1
\]
The equilibrium output of firm 2 is
\[
y_2^*
=
\frac{50\times8.3604}
{1+4.0990}
\approx81.9804
\]
The numerical equilibrium can be computed directly with the GEMB high-level framework. Firm 1 is represented as a joint-production activity, while firm 2 is represented by the degree-one homogeneous production function \(g(x_3,x_4,c_s)\) together with production stationarity conditions. The pollution price is allowed to be negative, whereas the consumer supplies one unit of the scale claim. The computed equilibrium reproduces the analytical solution above.



Listing 1: A \(5\times3\) Production-Externality Equilibrium Model with Degree-One Homogenization


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

alpha1 = 2.5
alpha2 = 50.0
theta = 1.0
omega = 10.0
beta = 0.5

# Degree-one homogenization of firm 2:
# g(q, l, cs) = alpha2 * cs * l / (cs + theta * q)
production_function = inputs -> begin
    q, l, cs = inputs
    alpha2 * cs * l / (cs + theta * q)
end

marginal_product_function = inputs -> begin
    q, l, cs = inputs
    denominator = cs + theta * q

    [
        -theta * alpha2 * cs * l / denominator^2,
        alpha2 * cs / denominator,
        theta * alpha2 * q * l / denominator^2,
    ]
end

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :product1;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
        :product2,
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :pollution;
            price_lower_bound=-Inf,
            price_upper_bound=Inf,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :scale_claim;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=:product2,
    numeraire_value=1.0,
)

# Firm 1:
# one unit of labor produces alpha1 units of product 1
# and alpha1 units of pollution.
firm1_spec = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (z, prices) -> [z],
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    firm1_spec;
    outputs=[:product1, :pollution],
    output_coefficients=[alpha1, alpha1],
    demands=:labor,
    activity_start=3.0,
    name=:firm1,
)

# Firm 2:
# pollution, labor, and scale claim are the three inputs.
GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.ProductionFunctionSpec(
        production_function,
        marginal_product_function;
        behavior=:stationary,
    );
    outputs=:product2,
    demands=[:pollution, :labor, :scale_claim],
    activity_start=60.0,
    demand_start=[3.0, 6.0, 0.8],
    demand_lower_bounds=[1.0e-10, 1.0e-10, 1.0e-10],
    production_multiplier_start=0.8,
    name=:firm2,
)

# Consumer:
# Cobb-Douglas preferences over products 1 and 2,
# with 10 units of labor and one unit of scale claim.
GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.CESSpec(
        [beta, 1.0 - beta];
        es=1.0,
        alpha=1.0,
    );
    demands=[:product1, :product2],
    endowments=[:labor, :scale_claim],
    endowment_quantities=[omega, 1.0],
    activity_start=15.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    p0=[10.0, 1.0, -5.0, 5.0, 20.0],
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(
    model,
    result;
    display_tol=1.0e-9,
    sigdigits=8,
)

l1 = result.agent_variable_values[1][1]

_, pollution_input, l2, scale_claim_input, _ =
    result.agent_variable_values[2]

w = omega * result.prices[4] +
    result.prices[5]

println("\nLabor inputs:")
println("l1 = ", l1)
println("l2 = ", l2)

println("\nFirm 2 inputs:")
println("pollution = ", pollution_input)
println("scale claim = ", scale_claim_input)

println("\nPrices:")
println(result.prices)

println("\nConsumer income:")
println(w)

title: Production Externality
text:
Uninternalized Production Externality
Now consider the case in which the production externality is not internalized. Firm 1 generates pollution as a by-product of producing product 1, and the pollution lowers the productivity of firm 2. Since pollution is not priced or traded in this case, it need not be included explicitly as a commodity. Its effect can instead be represented directly through the dependence of firm 2’s production technology on the activity level of firm 1.
Assume the following:

There are three commodities: product 1, product 2, and labor; and there are two firms and one consumer. Product 2 is the numeraire.
Firm 1 produces product 1. One unit of labor produces \(\alpha_1\) units of product 1 and simultaneously generates \(\alpha_1\) units of pollution. If its labor input is \(\ell_1\), its output of product 1 and the associated pollution are therefore both \(\alpha_1\ell_1\).
Firm 2 produces product 2 using labor. Its productivity is negatively affected by the pollution generated by firm 1. If its labor input is \(\ell_2\), its output is

\[
y_2
=
\frac{\alpha_2\ell_2}
{1+\theta\alpha_1\ell_1}
\]

The pollution generated by firm 1 is an external effect on firm 2 and carries no price.
The consumer has Cobb–Douglas preferences

\[
u(x_1,x_2)
=
x_1^\beta x_2^{1-\beta},
\qquad
0<\beta<1
\]
and is endowed with \(\omega\) units of labor.
Retaining the commodity indices from the previous formulation, let the reduced price vector be
\[
\mathbf p
=
(p_1,1,p_4)^\top
\]
and let \(\mathbf l=(\ell_1,\ell_2)^\top\). The demand and supply matrices can be written as
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\mathbf l,w)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0&\frac{\beta w}{p_1}\\
0&0&(1-\beta)w\\
\ell_1&\ell_2&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf S(\mathbf l)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\alpha_1\ell_1&0&0\\
0&\frac{\alpha_2\ell_2}{1+\theta\alpha_1\ell_1}&0\\
0&0&\omega
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The production externality therefore enters the equilibrium system through the supply of product 2. Firm 2 takes the activity of firm 1, and hence the resulting pollution level, as given. Because pollution is not a traded commodity, no pollution expenditure appears in the revenue-expenditure balance condition of either firm.
Solving the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model gives
\[
\mathbf l^*
=
\left(
\beta\omega,
(1-\beta)\omega
\right)^\top
\]
and
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
\left(
\frac{\alpha_2}
{\alpha_1(1+\theta\alpha_1\beta\omega)},
1,
\frac{\alpha_2}
{1+\theta\alpha_1\beta\omega}
\right)^\top
\]
The equilibrium income of the consumer is
\[
w^*
=
\frac{\alpha_2\omega}
{1+\theta\alpha_1\beta\omega}
\]
For comparison with the previous formulation, one may append a zero pollution price, \(p_3=0\). The corresponding price vector is therefore
\[
\left(
\frac{\alpha_2}
{\alpha_1(1+\theta\alpha_1\beta\omega)},
1,
0,
\frac{\alpha_2}
{1+\theta\alpha_1\beta\omega}
\right)^\top
\]
For
\[
\alpha_1=2.5,
\qquad
\alpha_2=50,
\qquad
\theta=1,
\qquad
\omega=10,
\qquad
\beta=0.5
\]
the equilibrium is (see Wiesmeth, 2012, p. 65)
\[
\mathbf l^*
=
(5,5)^\top
\]
and the reduced equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
\left(
\frac{40}{27},
1,
\frac{100}{27}
\right)^\top
\approx
(1.4815,1,3.7037)^\top
\]
The consumer’s equilibrium income is
\[
w^*
=
\frac{1000}{27}
\approx37.0370
\]
Firm 1 produces
\[
y_1^*
=
\alpha_1\ell_1^*
=
12.5
\]
while firm 2 produces
\[
y_2^*
=
\frac{50\times5}{1+2.5\times5}
=
\frac{500}{27}
\approx18.5185
\]
The corresponding consumer demands are
\[
x_1^*
=
12.5,
\qquad
x_2^*
=
\frac{500}{27}
\]
so both product markets clear.
In the GEMB implementation, the pollution commodity is omitted altogether. Firm 2 instead observes the activity level of firm 1, and its labor requirement is specified as
\[
\ell_2
=
\frac{1+\theta\alpha_1\ell_1}{\alpha_2}y_2
\]
Thus, the externality affects firm 2’s production technology without being represented as a priced transaction. The numerical implementation in Listing 2 reproduces the analytical equilibrium above.



Listing 2: A \(3\times3\) Equilibrium Model with an Uninternalized Production Externality


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

alpha1 = 2.5
alpha2 = 50.0
theta = 1.0
omega = 10.0
beta = 0.5

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :product1;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
        :product2,
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=:product2,
    numeraire_value=1.0,
)

# Firm 1:
# one unit of labor produces alpha1 units of product 1.
firm1_spec = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (z, prices) -> [z],
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    firm1_spec;
    outputs=:product1,
    output_coefficients=alpha1,
    demands=:labor,
    activity_start=3.0,
    name=:firm1,
)

# Firm 2:
# its labor requirement depends on firm 1's activity through
# the production externality.
firm2_spec = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (y, prices, observed_values) -> begin
        l1 = observed_values[1]

        [
            y * (1.0 + theta * alpha1 * l1) / alpha2
        ]
    end,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    firm2_spec;
    outputs=:product2,
    demands=:labor,
    observed_variables=[
        GEMB.agent_variable_ref(:firm1, :activity),
    ],
    activity_start=20.0,
    name=:firm2,
)

# Consumer:
# Cobb-Douglas preferences over products 1 and 2.
GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.CESSpec(
        [beta, 1.0 - beta];
        es=1.0,
        alpha=1.0,
    );
    demands=[:product1, :product2],
    endowments=:labor,
    endowment_quantities=omega,
    activity_start=10.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    p0=[1.0, 1.0, 2.0],
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(
    model,
    result;
    display_tol=1.0e-9,
    sigdigits=8,
)

stats = GEMB.equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

l1 = stats.activity_levels[1]
y2 = stats.activity_levels[2]
l2 = y2 * (1.0 + theta * alpha1 * l1) / alpha2
w = omega * result.prices[3]

p_full = [
    result.prices[1],
    result.prices[2],
    0.0,
    result.prices[3],
]

println("\nLabor allocation:")
println("l1 = ", l1)
println("l2 = ", l2)

println("\nFull price vector (including pollution price p3 = 0):")
println(p_full)

println("\nConsumer income:")
println(w)

The economy contains four commodities and four economic agents. The commodities are one product and three primary factors, while the economic agents are three firms and one consumer. The product is taken as the numeraire commodity.

\mathbf A(u)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0&0&u\\
8&6&1&0\\
4&2&1.5&0\\
2&1.5&0.5&0

and

\mathbf B
=
\begin{bmatrix}
60&30&20&0\\
0&0&0&48\\
0&0&0&20\\
0&0&0&8
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The consumer demands only the product. Its utility level \(u\) is equal to the quantity of the product consumed. Hence maximizing utility is equivalent to maximizing total product output.
The consumer supplies \(48\), \(20\), and \(8\) units of the three primary factors, respectively.

\[
\mathbf p=(1,p_2,p_3,p_4)^\top
\]
be the price vector and

the activity-level vector, where \(z_1,z_2,z_3\) are the activity levels of the three firms and the consumer population is normalized to one.

\[
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf A(u)
\geq
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf B
\] \[
\mathbf A(u)\mathbf z
\leq
\mathbf B\mathbf z
\]
The equilibrium is
\[
(z_1^*,z_2^*,z_3^*)
=
(2,0,8)
\]
with

title: General Equilibrium and Linear Programming
section: Primal and Dual Linear Programming Problems
text:
Primal and Dual Linear Programming Problems
The structural equilibrium model above simultaneously characterizes the solutions to the primal and dual linear programming problems corresponding to the Dakota Furniture Company example in Winston (2003). Define
\[
\mathbf z_f=(z_1,z_2,z_3)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf b=(60,30,20)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf e=(48,20,8)^\top
\]
and the input-coefficient matrix
\[
\mathbf A_f
=
\begin{bmatrix}
8&6&1\\
4&2&1.5\\
2&1.5&0.5
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The primal linear programming problem is
\[
\max_{\mathbf z_f\geq\mathbf0}
\mathbf b^\top\mathbf z_f
\qquad
\text{s.t.}
\qquad
\mathbf A_f\mathbf z_f\leq\mathbf e
\]
Its dual problem is
\[
\min_{\mathbf p_f\geq\mathbf0}
\mathbf p_f^\top\mathbf e
\qquad
\text{s.t.}
\qquad
\mathbf p_f^\top\mathbf A_f\geq\mathbf b^\top
\]
where
\[
\mathbf p_f=(p_2,p_3,p_4)^\top
\]
is the vector of primary-factor prices, with the product price normalized to one.
The equilibrium firm activity levels
\[
\mathbf z_f^*=(2,0,8)^\top
\]
solve the primal problem, while the equilibrium factor prices
\[
\mathbf p_f^*=(0,10,10)^\top
\]
solve the dual problem. The optimal values of the two problems are equal:
\[
\mathbf b^\top\mathbf z_f^*
=
\mathbf p_f^{*\top}\mathbf e
=
280
\]
Thus, solving the structural equilibrium model simultaneously solves the primal allocation problem and the dual pricing problem.
In the GEMB numerical representation, the consumer population is not represented by a separate activity variable. Instead, the consumer’s activity level represents its utility level. The resulting activity levels are therefore
\[
(2,0,8,280)
\]
for the three firms and the consumer, respectively.



Listing 1: A \(4\times4\) General Equilibrium Representation of a Linear Programming Problem


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

input_coefficients = [
    8.0  6.0  1.0
    4.0  2.0  1.5
    2.0  1.5  0.5
]

output_coefficients = [60.0, 30.0, 20.0]
factor_endowments = [48.0, 20.0, 8.0]
factors = [:factor_1, :factor_2, :factor_3]

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [:product, factors...];
    numeraire=:product,
)

for j in 1:3
    coefficients = input_coefficients[:, j]

    production = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
        (z, p) -> z .* coefficients,
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        production;
        outputs=:product,
        output_coefficients=output_coefficients[j],
        demands=factors,
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("firm_", j),
    )
end

consumer = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (u, p) -> [u],
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    consumer;
    demands=:product,
    endowments=factors,
    endowment_quantities=factor_endowments,
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    silent=true,

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

title: Monopolistic Supply
text:
Assume the following (see Li, 2019, p. 146):

The economy contains two commodities and two consumers. Commodity 2 is the numeraire commodity, so the price vector is
\[
\mathbf p=(p_1,1)^\top
\]
Consumer 1 is endowed with \(s_1>0\) units of commodity 1, while consumer 2 is endowed with \(s_2>0\) units of commodity 2. The endowment matrix is

\[
\mathbf S=
\begin{bmatrix}
s_1&0\\
0&s_2
\end{bmatrix}
\]

The two consumers have the same reduced-form CES utility function
\[
u(x_1,x_2)
=
(x_1^{-1}+x_2^{-1})^{-1}
\]
In the competitive benchmark, both consumers supply their full endowments. In the monopoly case, consumer 1 may choose to supply only \(q\) units of commodity 1, where \(0<q\leq s_1\), while the remaining \(s_1-q\) units are left idle. The production process and the consumption of final products are omitted in this simplified model. Accordingly, the CES utility function is a reduced-form representation of the utility generated through the omitted production and final-product consumption process, while the two commodities themselves represent production factors. Consumer 2 continues to supply its full endowment.

For the above utility function, the demand matrix can be written as
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\mathbf u)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_1\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right)
&
u_2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right)
\\
u_1(1+\sqrt{p_1})
&
u_2(1+\sqrt{p_1})
\end{bmatrix}
\]

title: Monopolistic Supply
text:
Analytical Solution
Under full endowment supply, solving the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model gives
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
\left(
\left(\frac{s_2}{s_1}\right)^2,
1
\right)^\top
\]
and
\[
u_1^*
=
\frac{s_1s_2^2}{(s_1+s_2)^2},
\qquad
u_2^*
=
\frac{s_2s_1^2}{(s_1+s_2)^2}
\]
For fixed \(s_2\), consumer 1’s equilibrium utility satisfies
\[
\frac{d u_1^*}{d s_1}
=
\frac{s_2^2(s_2-s_1)}{(s_1+s_2)^3}
\]
Hence \(u_1^*\) increases with \(s_1\) when \(s_1<s_2\), decreases with \(s_1\) when \(s_1>s_2\), and reaches its maximum at \(s_1=s_2\).
For any given supply level \(q\) chosen by consumer 1, where \(0<q\leq s_1\), the resulting competitive equilibrium is obtained by replacing \(s_1\) with \(q\). Thus,
\[
p_1(q)
=
\left(\frac{s_2}{q}\right)^2
\]
and consumer 1’s equilibrium utility is
\[
u_1(q)
=
\frac{q s_2^2}{(q+s_2)^2}
\]
The monopoly supply problem is therefore
\[
\max_{0<q\leq s_1}u_1(q)
\]
Since
\[
\frac{d u_1}{dq}
=
\frac{s_2^2(s_2-q)}{(q+s_2)^3}
\]
the optimal supply is
\[
q^*
=
\min\{s_1,s_2\}
\]
In particular, if \(s_1>s_2\),
\[
q^*=s_2<s_1
\]
so consumer 1 increases its equilibrium utility by withholding part of its endowment from the market.
For example, let
\[
s_1=200,
\qquad
s_2=100
\]
Under full supply, the competitive equilibrium is
\[
\mathbf p^*=(0.25,1)^\top
\]
with
\[
u_1^*=22.2222,
\qquad
u_2^*=44.4444
\]
The monopoly solution is
\[
q^*=100
\]
which gives
\[
\mathbf p^*=(1,1)^\top
\]
and
\[
u_1^*=u_2^*=25
\]
Consumer 1 therefore raises its equilibrium utility from approximately \(22.2222\) to \(25\) by reducing its supply from \(200\) to \(100\).

title: Monopolistic Supply
text:
Numerical Solution
The numerical solution treats the monopoly problem as a hierarchical equilibrium problem. For each candidate supply \(q\), the inner problem constructs the corresponding pure-exchange economy and solves its competitive equilibrium with GEMB. The resulting equilibrium utility of consumer 1 is then returned to the outer optimization problem. The numerical procedure can be summarized as
\[
q
\longrightarrow
\text{competitive equilibrium}
\longrightarrow
\mathbf p^*(q),\mathbf u^*(q)
\longrightarrow
u_1^*(q)
\longrightarrow
\max_q u_1^*(q)
\]
With \(s_1=200\) and \(s_2=100\), the numerical solution gives
\[
q^*\approx100,
\qquad
\mathbf p^*\approx(1,1)^\top
\]
and
\[
u_1^*\approx25,
\qquad
u_2^*\approx25
\]
which agrees with the analytical solution.



Listing 1: A \(2\times2\) Pure-Exchange Monopoly Model with Hierarchical Equilibrium


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling
using Optim

s1 = 200.0
s2 = 100.0

# u(x1, x2) = (x1^(-1) + x2^(-1))^(-1)
const preference = GEMB.CESSpec(
    [1.0, 1.0];
    es=0.5,
)

function solve_competitive_equilibrium(q, s2)
    model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
        [
            GEMB.CommoditySpec(
                :commodity_1;
                price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
            ),
            :commodity_2,
        ];
        numeraire=:commodity_2,
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        preference;
        demands=[:commodity_1, :commodity_2],
        endowments=:commodity_1,
        endowment_quantities=q,
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=:consumer_1,
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        preference;
        demands=[:commodity_1, :commodity_2],
        endowments=:commodity_2,
        endowment_quantities=s2,
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=:consumer_2,
    )

    result = GEMB.solve(
        model;
        silent=true,
    )

    u1 = result.agent_variable_values[1][1]
    u2 = result.agent_variable_values[2][1]

    return (
        model=model,
        result=result,
        u1=u1,
        u2=u2,
    )
end

function monopoly_objective(q)
    equilibrium = solve_competitive_equilibrium(q, s2)
    return -equilibrium.u1
end

# Prevent inner equilibrium breakdown at q = 0
q_lower = 0.01 * s1

optimization = optimize(
    monopoly_objective,
    q_lower,
    s1,
    Brent();
    rel_tol=1.0e-8,
    abs_tol=1.0e-8,
)

q_star = Optim.minimizer(optimization)

baseline = solve_competitive_equilibrium(s1, s2)
monopoly = solve_competitive_equilibrium(q_star, s2)

println("========== Baseline competitive equilibrium ==========")
println("Supply of consumer 1 = ", s1)
println("Prices = ", baseline.result.prices)
println("Utility of consumer 1 = ", baseline.u1)
println("Utility of consumer 2 = ", baseline.u2)

println("\n========== Monopoly equilibrium ==========")
println("Optimal supply of consumer 1 = ", q_star)
println("Prices = ", monopoly.result.prices)
println("Utility of consumer 1 = ", monopoly.u1)
println("Utility of consumer 2 = ", monopoly.u2)
println("Outer optimization converged = ", Optim.converged(optimization))

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(
    monopoly.model,
    monopoly.result,
)

title: Introduction
text:
The book GeneralEquilibriumModeling.jl and Structural Equilibrium Models presents a collection of basic applied general equilibrium models together with numerical solution programs based on GeneralEquilibriumModeling.jl.
This collection presents further applied economic models. Most of them are formulated mathematically as structural equilibrium models and solved numerically using the Julia package GeneralEquilibriumModeling.jl and the R package GE.

title: Introduction
text:
Introduction to Structural Equilibrium Models
The strict-sense structural equilibrium model extends the input and output coefficient matrices of the von Neumann equilibrium model to unit demand and unit supply matrices that may depend on prices, utility levels, and activity levels (Li, 2019, chap. 3). After incorporating any discount factor into the unit supply matrix, it can be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf A(\cdot)
&\geq
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf B(\cdot)\\
\mathbf A(\cdot)\mathbf z
&\leq
\mathbf B(\cdot)\mathbf z
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\mathbf p\geq\mathbf 0\) is the price vector and \(\mathbf z\geq\mathbf 0\) is the activity-level vector. The first condition represents unit revenue-expenditure balance, and the second represents supply-demand balance (i.e., market clearing).
The mixed-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model is written directly in terms of the demand and supply matrices of economic agents:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf D(\cdot)
&=
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf S(\cdot)\\
\mathbf D(\cdot)\mathbf 1
&\leq
\mathbf S(\cdot)\mathbf 1
\end{aligned}
\]
The first condition represents total revenue-expenditure balance for each economic agent, while the second states that aggregate demand for each commodity does not exceed aggregate supply.
If no commodity is in excess supply at equilibrium, the model becomes the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf D(\cdot)
&=
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf S(\cdot)\\
\mathbf D(\cdot)\mathbf 1
&=
\mathbf S(\cdot)\mathbf 1
\end{aligned}
\]
Here, every economic agent satisfies total revenue-expenditure balance, and supply equals demand for every commodity.

For details, see The von Neumann Equilibrium Model and Structural Equilibrium Models.

title: Excess Burden of a Commodity Tax under Quasilinear Utility Functions
text:
This example is essentially a pure exchange economy, with a tax intermediary added to implement the commodity tax.
Assume the following:

The economy contains four commodities: corn, iron, taxed iron, and tax certificates; and four economic agents: consumer 1, consumer 2, a firm, and the government. Corn is taken as the numeraire commodity.
Consumer 1 has the utility function
\[
u_1(x_1,x_3)
=
x_1+\beta_1\left(\alpha_1x_3-\frac12x_3^2\right)
\]
where \(x_1\) denotes corn, \(x_3\) denotes taxed iron, and \(\alpha_1,\beta_1>0\). Consumer 1 is endowed with \(\omega_1\) units of corn.
Consumer 2 has the utility function
\[
u_2(x_1,x_2)
=
x_1+\beta_2\left(\alpha_2x_2-\frac12x_2^2\right)
\]
where \(x_1\) denotes corn, \(x_2\) denotes iron, and \(\alpha_2,\beta_2>0\). Consumer 2 is endowed with \(\omega_2\) units of iron. Consumer 1 wishes to purchase iron supplied by consumer 2, and the government imposes a commodity tax on iron.
The firm acts as a tax agency. It uses iron and tax certificates as inputs to produce taxed iron. Under the tax system, consumer 1 must purchase taxed iron from the firm, while consumer 2 must sell iron through the firm.
The government is endowed with one unit of the tax certificate and has the utility function \(u_G=x_1\).

where \(x_1\) denotes corn, \(x_2\) denotes iron, and \(\alpha_2,\beta_2>0\). Consumer 2 is endowed with \(\omega_2\) units of iron. Consumer 1 wishes to purchase iron supplied by consumer 2, and the government imposes a commodity tax on iron.
The firm acts as a tax agency. It uses iron and tax certificates as inputs to produce taxed iron. Under the tax system, consumer 1 must purchase taxed iron from the firm, while consumer 2 must sell iron through the firm.
The government is endowed with one unit of the tax certificate and has the utility function \(u_G=x_1\).

title: Excess Burden of a Commodity Tax under Quasilinear Utility Functions
text:
Equilibrium
Suppose the parameter values ensure interior solutions in both the taxed and no-tax equilibria, with positive consumption of corn and iron-related commodities for both consumers and positive equilibrium prices for \(\tau>0\). Consumer 1’s demand for taxed iron is
\[
x_3(p_3)
=
\alpha_1-\frac{p_3}{\beta_1}
\]
and consumer 2’s demand for iron is
\[
x_2(p_2)
=
\alpha_2-\frac{p_2}{\beta_2}
\]
Let the price vector be
\[
\mathbf p:=(1,p_2,p_3,p_4)^\top
\]
where \(p_2\) is the price of iron, \(p_3\) is the price of taxed iron, and \(p_4\) is the price of the tax certificate. Let \(y\) denote the firm’s activity level, which is also its output of taxed iron; let \(\mathbf w=(w_1,w_2)^\top\) denote the vector of consumer incomes; let \(u\) denote the government’s utility level; and let \(\tau>0\) denote the ad valorem commodity tax rate.
Consumer 1 purchases \(x_3\) units of taxed iron, so its demand for corn is \(w_1-p_3x_3\). Consumer 2 consumes \(x_2\) units of iron and sells the remaining iron, so its demand for corn is \(w_2-p_2x_2\).
To produce one unit of taxed iron, the firm uses one unit of iron and tax certificates with a total value equal to \(\tau p_2\). Therefore, producing \(y\) units of taxed iron requires
\[
\frac{yp_2\tau}{p_4}
\]
units of tax certificates.
The government sells its endowment of tax certificates and spends the resulting income entirely on corn.
The demand matrix is therefore
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,u,\mathbf w,y)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
w_1-p_3x_3 & w_2-p_2x_2 & 0 & u\\
0 & x_2 & y & 0\\
x_3 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & \frac{yp_2\tau}{p_4} & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and the supply matrix is
\[
\mathbf S(y)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & \omega_2 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & y & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Solving the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model gives
\[
p_2^*
=
\frac{
\beta_1\beta_2(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\omega_2)
}{
\beta_1+(1+\tau)\beta_2
}
\]
\[
p_3^*
=
(1+\tau)p_2^*
\]
and
\[
p_4^*
=
y^*p_2^*\tau
\]
The equilibrium quantity of taxed iron is
\[
y^*
=
\alpha_1-\frac{p_3^*}{\beta_1}
\]
with
\[
x_3^*=y^*
\]
and
\[
x_2^*
=
\alpha_2-\frac{p_2^*}{\beta_2}
\]
The equilibrium consumer incomes and government utility level are
\[
w_1^*=\omega_1
\]
\[
w_2^*=p_2^*\omega_2
\]
and
\[
u^*=p_4^*
\]
respectively.
The commodity tax generates a wedge between the buyer’s price and the seller’s price:
\[
p_3^*-p_2^*
=
\tau p_2^*
\]
Consider the parameter values
\[
\beta_1=\beta_2=0.05,\qquad
\alpha_1=120,\qquad
\alpha_2=100
\]
\[
\omega_1=1000,\qquad
\omega_2=100,\qquad
\tau=1
\]
The analytical solution is
\[
p_2^*=2,\qquad
p_3^*=4,\qquad
p_4^*=80
\]
and
\[
y^*=40
\]
Hence the equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
(1,2,4,80)^\top
\]
Consumer 1 consumes 840 units of corn and 40 units of taxed iron. Consumer 2 consumes 80 units of corn and 60 units of iron. The government consumes 80 units of corn.

title: Excess Burden of a Commodity Tax under Quasilinear Utility Functions
section: Excess Burden of the Commodity Tax
text:
Excess Burden of the Commodity Tax
The equilibrium utilities of the two consumers under the commodity tax rate \(\tau\) are
\[
u_1^*(\tau)
=
\omega_1-p_3^*x_3^*
+
\beta_1
\left(
\alpha_1x_3^*
-\frac12(x_3^*)^2
\right)
\]
and
\[
u_2^*(\tau)
=
p_2^*(\omega_2-x_2^*)
+
\beta_2
\left(
\alpha_2x_2^*
-\frac12(x_2^*)^2
\right)
\]
The government’s equilibrium utility is
\[
u_G^*(\tau)
=
u^*
=
p_4^*
=
y^*p_2^*\tau
\]
Since the three utility functions are normalized in units of corn, define the utilitarian social welfare measure under the commodity tax rate \(\tau\) as
\[
W(\tau)
:=
u_1^*(\tau)
+
u_2^*(\tau)
+
u_G^*(\tau)
\]
Let \(W(0)\) denote social welfare in the no-tax equilibrium. The excess burden of the commodity tax is
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
\]
which can be calculated as
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
=
\frac{
\beta_1^2\beta_2^2\tau^2
(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\omega_2)^2
}{
2(\beta_1+\beta_2)
\left[\beta_1+\beta_2(1+\tau)\right]^2
}
\]
Using the equilibrium price \(p_2^*\), this can be written more simply as
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
=
\frac{(\tau p_2^*)^2}
{2(\beta_1+\beta_2)}
\]
The reduction in the equilibrium quantity of traded iron relative to the no-tax equilibrium is
\[
y^*(0)-y^*(\tau)
=
\frac{\tau p_2^*}{\beta_1+\beta_2}
\]
while the commodity-tax wedge is
\[
p_3^*-p_2^*
=
\tau p_2^*
\]
Hence the excess burden can also be expressed as
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
=
\frac12
(p_3^*-p_2^*)
\left[y^*(0)-y^*(\tau)\right]
\]
which is the area of the excess-burden triangle generated by the commodity tax.
For the numerical parameter values above, the no-tax equilibrium quantity is
\[
y^*(0)=60
\]
while the equilibrium quantity under \(\tau=1\) is
\[
y^*(1)=40
\]
The commodity-tax wedge is
\[
p_3^*-p_2^*=2
\]
and therefore the excess burden is
\[
\frac12(60-40)(4-2)=20
\]
Equivalently,
\[
W(0)=1430,\qquad
W(1)=1410
\]
so that
\[
W(0)-W(1)=20
\]
When \(\tau=0\), the tax certificate has no economic role and its equilibrium price is zero, while the term \(\frac{yp_2\tau}{p_4}\) in the demand matrix becomes indeterminate. The no-tax equilibrium should therefore be represented without the tax-certificate commodity, or equivalently interpreted through the limit as \(\tau\to0^+\) when welfare is considered.
The corresponding GEMB implementation is given in Listing 1.



Listing 1: A \(4\times4\) General Equilibrium Model with a Commodity Tax and Quasilinear Utility Functions


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

beta1 = 0.05
beta2 = 0.05
alpha1 = 120.0
alpha2 = 100.0

omega1 = 1000.0
omega2 = 100.0

tau = 1.0

consumer1_demand = (income, p) -> begin
    p1, p3 = p
    x3 = alpha1 - p3 / (beta1 * p1)
    x1 = (income - p3 * x3) / p1
    [x1, x3]
end

consumer2_demand = (income, p) -> begin
    p1, p2 = p
    x2 = alpha2 - p2 / (beta2 * p1)
    x1 = (income - p2 * x2) / p1
    [x1, x2]
end

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        :corn,
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :iron;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :taxed_iron;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :tax_certificate;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=:corn,
    numeraire_value=1.0,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.MarshallDemandConsumerSpec(consumer1_demand);
    demands=[:corn, :taxed_iron],
    endowments=:corn,
    endowment_quantities=omega1,
    name=:consumer1,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.MarshallDemandConsumerSpec(consumer2_demand);
    demands=[:corn, :iron],
    endowments=:iron,
    endowment_quantities=omega2,
    name=:consumer2,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.CESSpec(
        [1.0];
        es=0.0,
        alpha=1.0,
    );
    outputs=:taxed_iron,
    demands=:iron,
    claim_rate=tau,
    claim=GEMB.CommodityRef(:tax_certificate),
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:tax_agency,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.CESSpec(
        [1.0];
        es=0.0,
        alpha=1.0,
    );
    demands=:corn,
    endowments=:tax_certificate,
    endowment_quantities=1.0,
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:government,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    p0=[1.0, 1.5, 3.0, 60.0],
    residual_tol=1.0e-10,
    silent=true,
)

stats = GEMB.equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

title: Minimum-Wage and Endogenous Labor Supply
text:
Assume the following:

The economy contains three commodities and two economic agents, a firm and a consumer. The commodities are product, labor, and land. The product is taken as the numeraire commodity.
The firm uses labor and land to produce the product according to the constant-returns-to-scale production function
\[
y=\alpha l^\beta t^{1-\beta},
\qquad
\alpha>0,\quad0<\beta<1
\]
where \(l\) and \(t\) denote labor and land inputs, respectively.
The consumer supplies labor and land and demands only the product. Its product demand is denoted by \(c\). The land supply \(\bar t>0\) is exogenous, whereas the labor supply \(s\geq0\) is endogenous.
Assume that labor is abundant and that the minimum wage is binding. The minimum wage may be legally mandated or determined by the subsistence level. In the model, the labor price is fixed exogenously at the minimum wage \(\bar w>0\), and the endogenous labor supply \(s\) adjusts so that the labor market clears at this fixed wage. In other words, only part of the available labor enters the market, while the remainder stays outside the market.

Let the price vector be
\[
\mathbf p=(1,w,r)^\top
\]
where \(w\) and \(r\) are the prices of labor and land, respectively. Given \(y\), \(c\), \(s\), \(w\), and \(r\), the demand and supply matrices can be written explicitly as
\[
\mathbf D(y,c,w,r)=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&
c\\[6pt]
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\beta r}{(1-\beta)w}
\right)^{1-\beta}
&
0\\[10pt]
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{(1-\beta)w}{\beta r}
\right)^\beta
&
0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf S(y,s)=
\begin{bmatrix}
y&0\\
0&s\\
0&\bar t
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The wide-sense structural equilibrium model is
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf D(y,w,r)=\mathbf p^\top\mathbf S(y)\\
\mathbf D(y,w,r)\mathbf 1=\mathbf S(y)\mathbf 1\\
w=\bar w
\end{cases}
\]
where the third equation imposes the binding minimum-wage condition.

title: Minimum-Wage and Endogenous Labor Supply
text:
Equilibrium
The equilibrium labor supply is
\[
s^*
=
\bar t
\left(
\frac{\alpha\beta}{\bar w}
\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}
\]
and the corresponding equilibrium land price, output, and consumption are
\[
r^*
=
\alpha(1-\beta)
(s^*)^\beta\bar t^{-\beta}
\]
\[
y^*
=
\alpha(s^*)^\beta\bar t^{1-\beta}
\]
and
\[
c^*=y^*
\]
For the numerical example, let
\[
\alpha=2,
\qquad
\beta=0.5,
\qquad
\bar t=100,
\qquad
\bar w=2
\]
The equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*=(1,2,0.5)^\top
\]
and the equilibrium quantities are
\[
s^*=l^*=25,
\qquad
t^*=100,
\qquad
y^*=c^*=100
\]
Accordingly, the equilibrium demand and supply matrices are
\[
\mathbf D^*=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&100\\
25&0\\
100&0
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf S^*=
\begin{bmatrix}
100&0\\
0&25\\
0&100
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Thus, fixing the labor price at \(\bar w=2\) endogenously determines the equilibrium labor supply as \(s^*=25\).
The corresponding GEMB implementation is given in Listing Listing 1. The endogenous labor supply is represented by a condition variable paired with the fixed-wage condition. The consumer is represented by an ActivityDemandSpec: its activity level determines product consumption, while a customized output specification supplies the endogenous quantity of labor and the fixed quantity of land.



Listing 1: A \(3\times2\) Equilibrium Model with a Fixed Wage and Endogenous Labor Supply


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEM
using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
import GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB: activity_supply

alpha = 2.0
beta = 0.5
land_supply = 100.0
fixed_wage = 2.0

struct LaborLandSupplySpec <: AbstractActivitySupplySpec
    land_supply::Float64
end

function activity_supply(
    spec::LaborLandSupplySpec,
    activity,
    prices,
    observed_values,
)
    labor_supply = observed_values[1]
    [labor_supply, spec.land_supply]
end

model = GEMBModel(
    [
        :product,
        CommoditySpec(:labor; price_lower_bound=1.0e-6),
        CommoditySpec(:land; price_lower_bound=1.0e-6),
    ];
    numeraire=:product,
    numeraire_value=1.0,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    ConditionAgentSpec(
        (variables, observed_values) -> [
            observed_values[1] - fixed_wage,
        ],
    );
    variable_names=:labor_supply,
    variable_start=100.0,
    variable_lower_bounds=0.0,
    variable_upper_bounds=Inf,
    observed_variables=[
        PriceVariableRef(:labor),
    ],
    name=:labor_condition,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    CESSpec(
        [beta, 1.0 - beta];
        es=1.0,
        alpha=alpha,
    );
    outputs=:product,
    demands=[:labor, :land],
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:firm,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    ActivityDemandSpec(
        (activity, prices) -> [activity],
    );
    outputs=[:labor, :land],
    output_spec=LaborLandSupplySpec(land_supply),
    demands=:product,
    activity_start=100.0,
    observed_variables=[
        agent_variable_ref(:labor_condition, :labor_supply),
    ],
    condition_rule=TotalRevenueExpenditureBalanceConditions(),
    name=:consumer,
)

result = solve(
    model;
    p0=[1.0, 1.0, 1.0],
    residual_tol=1.0e-10,
    silent=true,
)

labor_supply = result.agent_variable_values[1][1]
firm_output = result.agent_variable_values[2][1]
consumer_consumption = result.agent_variable_values[3][1]

println("Solved: ", result.solved)
println("Prices [product, labor, land]: ", result.prices)
println("Labor supply: ", labor_supply)
println("Firm output: ", firm_output)
println("Consumer consumption: ", consumer_consumption)
println("Total net supply: ", result.total_net_supply)
