title: Finite-Horizon Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium
text:
Assume the following (see Torres, 2016, chap. 2):

The economy has \(n_p\) periods and \(n_p-1\) production intervals. A product firm operating in period \(t\) starts production at the beginning of the period and obtains its output at the end of period \(t\), or equivalently at the beginning of period \(t+1\). Commodities dated at different periods are treated as different commodities.
The economy contains three types of dated commodities: products, labor, and capital rentals. Product firms and capital-rental firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), and there is one intertemporal consumer. The product also serves as capital.
The product firm operating in period \(t\) rents capital \(k^{(t)}\) and employs labor \(x^{(t)}\) to produce the product available in period \(t+1\) according to

\[
y^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\left(k^{(t)}\right)^{\beta_1}
\left(x^{(t)}\right)^{1-\beta_1}
\]
where \(\beta_1=0.35\) and \(\alpha^{(t)}=1\) in the benchmark case.

The capital-rental firm purchases the current product as capital, supplies its use to the product firm, and carries the undepreciated capital into the next period. Thus, an activity level of \(k^{(t)}\) requires \(k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{product}^{(t)}\) and supplies \(k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{capital_rental}^{(t)}\) together with \((1-\delta)k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{product}^{(t+1)}\), where \(\delta=0.06\). Combining the two production activities, the total product supply generated in period \(t\) and available in period \(t+1\) is \(y^{(t+1)}+(1-\delta)k^{(t)}\).
The representative consumer initially owns \(k^{(1)}=286.6341\) units of product and is endowed with \(\omega=100\) units of labor in each production period. Under the post-payment wage assumption, labor supplied in period \(t\) and product consumed in period \(t+1\) enter the same single-period utility function. Letting \(\ell^{(t)}\) denote leisure,

\[
u^{(t)}
=
\left(c^{(t+1)}\right)^{\beta_2}
\left(\ell^{(t)}\right)^{1-\beta_2}
\]
where \(\beta_2=0.4\). In equilibrium, labor-market clearing implies \(\ell^{(t)}=\omega-x^{(t)}\).
The subjective discount factor is \(\varGamma=0.97\).

Without tail adjustment, the intertemporal utility is formed from the single-period utility levels with relative weights

\[
1,\varGamma,\varGamma^2,\ldots,\varGamma^{n_p-2}
\]
Since both the within-period and intertemporal elasticities of substitution equal one, the nested utility function can be represented by a single CESSpec. For a sufficiently long horizon, the middle part of the equilibrium path approaches the steady state, although the final periods are affected by the finite-horizon tail effect.



Listing 1: A \(3\times3\) Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium Model without Tail Adjustment


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

np = 100

discount_factor = 0.97
depreciation_rate = 0.06
capital_share = 0.35
consumption_share = 0.4

labor_endowment = 100.0
initial_capital = 286.6341

technology = ones(np - 1)

product(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:product; period=t)
labor(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)
capital_rental(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:capital_rental; period=t)

intertemporal_weights = discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 2))

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=1:np,),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :capital_rental;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=labor(1),
)

rental_spec = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (activity, prices) -> [activity],
)

for t in 1:(np - 1)
    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        GEMB.CESSpec(
            [capital_share, 1 - capital_share];
            es=1.0,
            alpha=technology[t],
        );
        outputs=product(t + 1),
        demands=[
            capital_rental(t),
            labor(t),
        ],
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("firm_$t"),
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        rental_spec;
        outputs=[
            capital_rental(t),
            product(t + 1),
        ],
        output_coefficients=[
            1.0,
            1 - depreciation_rate,
        ],
        demands=product(t),
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("rental_$t"),
    )
end

product_weights =
    consumption_share .* intertemporal_weights

labor_weights =
    (1 - consumption_share) .* intertemporal_weights

utility_weights =
    vcat(product_weights, labor_weights)
utility_weights ./= sum(utility_weights)

consumer_demands = vcat(
    [product(t) for t in 2:np],
    [labor(t) for t in 1:(np - 1)],
)

consumer_endowments = vcat(
    [product(1)],
    [labor(t) for t in 1:(np - 1)],
)

consumer_endowment_quantities = vcat(
    [initial_capital],
    fill(labor_endowment, np - 1),
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.CESSpec(
        utility_weights;
        es=1.0,
        alpha=1.0,
    );
    demands=consumer_demands,
    endowments=consumer_endowments,
    endowment_quantities=consumer_endowment_quantities,
    name=:consumer,
)

gross_return = 1 / discount_factor
target_mpk =
    gross_return - (1 - depreciation_rate)

capital_labor_ratio =
    (capital_share / target_mpk)^(1 / (1 - capital_share))

steady_mpl =
    (1 - capital_share) *
    capital_labor_ratio^capital_share

product_price_1 =
    1 / (discount_factor * steady_mpl)

product_p0 =
    product_price_1 .* discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 1))

labor_p0 =
    discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 2))

rental_p0 =
    product_p0[1:(np - 1)] .-
    (1 - depreciation_rate) .* product_p0[2:np]

p0 = vcat(
    product_p0,
    labor_p0,
    rental_p0,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;

title: Finite-Horizon Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium
text:
Assume the following (see Torres, 2016, chap. 2):

The economy has \(n_p\) periods and \(n_p-1\) production intervals. A product firm operating in period \(t\) starts production at the beginning of the period and obtains its output at the end of period \(t\), or equivalently at the beginning of period \(t+1\). Commodities dated at different periods are treated as different commodities.
The economy contains three types of dated commodities: products, labor, and capital rentals. Product firms and capital-rental firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), and there is one intertemporal consumer. The product also serves as capital.
The product firm operating in period \(t\) rents capital \(k^{(t)}\) and employs labor \(x^{(t)}\) to produce the product available in period \(t+1\) according to

\[
y^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\left(k^{(t)}\right)^{\beta_1}
\left(x^{(t)}\right)^{1-\beta_1}
\]
where \(\beta_1=0.35\) and \(\alpha^{(t)}=1\) in the benchmark case.

The capital-rental firm purchases the current product as capital, supplies its use to the product firm, and carries the undepreciated capital into the next period. Thus, an activity level of \(k^{(t)}\) requires \(k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{product}^{(t)}\) and supplies \(k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{capital_rental}^{(t)}\) together with \((1-\delta)k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{product}^{(t+1)}\), where \(\delta=0.06\). Combining the two production activities, the total product supply generated in period \(t\) and available in period \(t+1\) is \(y^{(t+1)}+(1-\delta)k^{(t)}\).
The representative consumer initially owns \(k^{(1)}=286.6341\) units of product and is endowed with \(\omega=100\) units of labor in each production period. Under the post-payment wage assumption, labor supplied in period \(t\) and product consumed in period \(t+1\) enter the same single-period utility function. Letting \(\ell^{(t)}\) denote leisure,

\[
u^{(t)}
=
\left(c^{(t+1)}\right)^{\beta_2}
\left(\ell^{(t)}\right)^{1-\beta_2}
\]
where \(\beta_2=0.4\). In equilibrium, labor-market clearing implies \(\ell^{(t)}=\omega-x^{(t)}\).
The subjective discount factor is \(\varGamma=0.97\).

Without tail adjustment, the intertemporal utility is formed from the single-period utility levels with relative weights

\[
1,\varGamma,\varGamma^2,\ldots,\varGamma^{n_p-2}
\]
Since both the within-period and intertemporal elasticities of substitution equal one, the nested utility function can be represented by a single CESSpec. For a sufficiently long horizon, the middle part of the equilibrium path approaches the steady state, although the final periods are affected by the finite-horizon tail effect.

title: Finite-Horizon Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium
text:
Equilibrium with Tail Adjustment
To mitigate the finite-horizon tail effect, an additional demand for the terminal product is introduced alongside the ordinary single-period utility components. Let \(\eta>0\) denote its endogenous weight. The intertemporal utility structure is
\[
U
\sim
\prod_{t=1}^{n_p-1}
\left(u^{(t)}\right)^{\varGamma^{t-1}}
\left(c^{(n_p)}\right)^\eta
\]
The ordinary single-period preferences and discount factors remain unchanged. When the nested Cobb–Douglas utility is represented by a single CESSpec, the weight on the terminal product becomes \(\beta_2\varGamma^{n_p-2}+\eta\).
Since capital is the state variable of the model, \(\eta\) is paired with the tail condition
\[
k^{(n_p-2)}
=
k^{(n_p-1)}
\]
Thus, the terminal weight is determined endogenously so that the last two capital stocks coincide.
With \(n_p=20\), the steady-state benchmark is approximately
\[
k^*=286.6,
\qquad
x^*=36.04,
\qquad
y^*=74.47,
\qquad
c^*=57.27
\]
The tail-adjusted equilibrium gives
\[
\eta=1.157,
\qquad
\frac{\eta}{\varGamma^{18}}
\approx2.002
\]
where \(\varGamma^{18}\) is the discount weight on the last ordinary single-period utility component. The last two capital stocks are
\[
k^{(18)}
=
k^{(19)}
=
286.6
\]



Listing 2: A \(3\times3\) Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium Model with Tail Adjustment


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

np = 20

discount_factor = 0.97
depreciation_rate = 0.06
capital_share = 0.35
consumption_share = 0.4

labor_endowment = 100.0
initial_capital = 286.6341

product(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:product; period=t)
labor(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)
capital_rental(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:capital_rental; period=t)

intertemporal_weights = discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 2))

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=1:np,),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,

            :capital_rental;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=labor(1),
)

rental_spec = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (activity, prices) -> [activity],
)

for t in 1:(np - 1)
    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        GEMB.CESSpec(
            [capital_share, 1 - capital_share];
            es=1.0,
            alpha=technology[t],
        );
        outputs=product(t + 1),
        demands=[
            capital_rental(t),
            labor(t),
        ],
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("firm_$t"),
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        rental_spec;
        outputs=[
            capital_rental(t),
            product(t + 1),
        ],
        output_coefficients=[
            1.0,
            1 - depreciation_rate,
        ],
        demands=product(t),
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("rental_$t"),
    )
end

consumer_commodities = vcat(
    [product(t) for t in 1:np],
    [labor(t) for t in 1:(np - 1)],
)

consumer_net_supply = function (
    local_variables,
    local_prices,
    observed_values=Any[],
)
    terminal_weight = local_variables[1]

    product_prices = local_prices[1:np]
    labor_prices = local_prices[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)]

    product_weights =
        consumption_share .* intertemporal_weights
    product_weights[end] += terminal_weight

    labor_weights =
        (1 - consumption_share) .* intertemporal_weights

    beta = vcat(product_weights, labor_weights)
    beta ./= sum(beta)

    income =
        product_prices[1] * initial_capital +
        labor_endowment * sum(labor_prices)

    demand_prices = vcat(
        product_prices[2:np],
        labor_prices,
    )

    demand = GEMB.CES_demand(
        beta,
        income,
        demand_prices;
        es=1.0,
    )

    T = promote_type(
        eltype(local_variables),
        eltype(local_prices),
    )
    supply = zeros(T, 2 * np - 1)

    supply[1] = initial_capital
    supply[2:np] .= -demand[1:(np - 1)]
    supply[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)] .=
        labor_endowment .- demand[np:(2 * np - 2)]

    return supply
end

tail_condition = function (
    local_variables,
    local_prices,
    net_supply,
    observed_values,
)
    return [observed_values[1] - observed_values[2]]
end

GEMB.add_net_supply_agent!(
    model,
    consumer_net_supply;
    commodities=consumer_commodities,
    variable_names=[:terminal_weight],
    variable_lower_bounds=[1.0e-8],
    variable_upper_bounds=[Inf],
    variable_start=[1.0],
    observed_variables=[
        GEM.AgentVariableRef(
            Symbol("rental_$(np - 2)"),
            :activity,

        GEM.AgentVariableRef(
            Symbol("rental_$(np - 1)"),
            :activity,

    condition_rule=GEM.ExplicitAgentConditions(
        tail_condition,

    name=:consumer,
)

target_mpk =
    gross_return - (1 - depreciation_rate)

capital_labor_ratio =
    (capital_share / target_mpk)^(1 / (1 - capital_share))

steady_mpl =
    (1 - capital_share) *
    capital_labor_ratio^capital_share

product_price_1 =
    1 / (discount_factor * steady_mpl)

product_p0 =
    product_price_1 .* discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 1))

labor_p0 =
    discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 2))

rental_p0 =
    product_p0[1:(np - 1)] .-
    (1 - depreciation_rate) .* product_p0[2:np]

p0 = vcat(
    product_p0,
    labor_p0,
    rental_p0,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

prices = result.prices

product_prices = prices[1:np]
labor_prices = prices[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)]
rental_prices = prices[(2 * np):(3 * np - 2)]

new_output = [
    result.agent_variable_values[2 * t - 1][1]
    for t in 1:(np - 1)
]

capital = [
    result.agent_variable_values[2 * t][1]
    for t in 1:(np - 1)

labor_input = [
    -result.agent_net_supplies[2 * t - 1][3]
    for t in 1:(np - 1)

product_demand =
    -consumer_supply[2:np]

labor_supply =
    consumer_supply[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)]

leisure =
    labor_endowment .- labor_supply

terminal_weight =
    result.agent_variable_values[end][1]

ordinary_last_weight =
    consumption_share * intertemporal_weights[end]

ordinary_consumption = copy(product_demand)
ordinary_consumption[end] *=
    ordinary_last_weight /
    (ordinary_last_weight + terminal_weight)

    product_demand[end] - ordinary_consumption[end]

    new_output .+
    (1 - depreciation_rate) .* capital

    "Terminal weight ratio: ",

title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Knowledge Production
text:
The basic mechanism of the model is closely related to the R&D-based growth literature. Romer (1990) treats technological change as the outcome of intentional R&D investment and emphasizes the allocation of productive resources to research, while Jones (1995) considers a more general knowledge-production process in which the creation of new knowledge may depend on both R&D inputs and the existing stock of knowledge. The linear additive R&D specification adopted here can be viewed as a simple special case in which the increment in the production-efficiency parameter is proportional to current R&D labor and independent of the existing level of technology.
Assume the following:

The economy has \(n_p\) periods. A firm operating in period \(t\) starts production at the beginning of the period and obtains its product at the end of period \(t\), or equivalently at the beginning of period \(t+1\). Hence there are \(n_p-1\) interperiod production activities. In general, an \(n_p\)-period model may contain \(n_p\) dated products, but in the present example the initial-period product supply and consumption are omitted. The product commodities are therefore \(product^{(2)},\ldots,product^{(n_p)}\).
The economy contains four types of dated commodities: products, labor, technology knowledge (i.e., production-efficiency parameters), and scale claims. Product firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), R&D firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), and there is one intertemporal consumer. Commodities dated at different periods are treated as different commodities.
The product firm operating in period \(t\) uses the production-efficiency parameter \(\alpha^{(t)}\) and production labor \(x^{(t)}\) to produce the product available in period \(t+1\) according to \(c^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}\). To represent this technology as a degree-one homogeneous production function, a scale claim \(c_s^{(t)}\) is introduced, giving

\[
g\left(\alpha^{(t)},x^{(t)},c_s^{(t)}\right)
=
\frac{\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}}{c_s^{(t)}}
\]
The product firm follows the marginal pricing principle.

The R&D firm operating in period \(t\) uses R&D labor \(\ell^{(t)}\) to increase production efficiency from period \(t+1\) onward. With R&D-efficiency parameter \(\bar\alpha>0\), one unit of R&D labor generates \(\bar\alpha\) units of each future production-efficiency parameter commodity (i.e., technology knowledge) within the production horizon. Hence \(\alpha^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}+\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), or equivalently

\[
\alpha^{(t)}
=
\alpha^{(1)}
+
\bar\alpha
\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\ell^{(s)},
\qquad
t=2,\ldots,n_p-1
\]

The consumer is endowed with \(\omega>0\) units of labor and one unit of the scale claim in each production period, together with \(\alpha^{(1)}\) units of each dated production-efficiency parameter commodity. Labor-market balance is \(x^{(t)}+\ell^{(t)}=\omega\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), while \(x^{(n_p-1)}=\omega\) because R&D in the last production period cannot affect production within the horizon.
The consumer consumes \(c^{(2)},\ldots,c^{(n_p)}\) and has intertemporal utility

\[
u
=
\sum_{t=2}^{n_p}\rho^t\ln c^{(t)},
\qquad
0<\rho<1
\]
For the infinite-horizon version of the model, the critical production-efficiency level for R&D is
\[
\alpha^*
=
\frac{\rho\bar\alpha\omega}{1-\rho}
\tag{1}\]
R&D is undertaken when \(\alpha^{(t)}<\alpha^*\) and ceases once the production-efficiency parameter reaches the critical level. In particular, if \(\alpha^{(1)}\geq\alpha^*\), there is no incentive to undertake R&D.
The finite horizon generates a terminal effect. R&D undertaken late in the horizon affects fewer future production periods, so the incentive to undertake R&D declines near the terminal period and eventually disappears.
For \(n_p=9\), \(\rho=0.8\), \(\alpha^{(1)}=0.01\), \(\bar\alpha=0.0001\), and \(\omega=100\), the equilibrium R&D-labor path is approximately \((43.02,33.09,23.10,10.99,0,0,0)\). The corresponding productivity increments \(\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}\) are approximately \((0.004302,0.003309,0.002310,0.001099,0,0,0)\). The resulting productivity path is
\[
\left(
\alpha^{(2)},\ldots,\alpha^{(8)}
\right)
=
\left(
0.01430,\,
0.01761,\,
0.01992,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102
\right)
\]
Thus positive R&D occurs only in the first four R&D periods.



Listing 1: A \(4\times3\) Technology-Accumulation Intertemporal Equilibrium Model with Additive R&D


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
using Plots

np = 9

rho = 0.8
alpha1 = 0.01
alpha_bar = 0.0001
omega = 100.0

np >= 3 || throw(ArgumentError("np must be at least 3."))

product(t) = CommodityRef(:product; period=t)

    rho * alpha_bar * omega / (1 - rho)

alpha_target_start = if alpha1 < alpha_star
    alpha_star .-
    (alpha_star - alpha1) .* rho .^ (0:(np - 2))
else
    fill(alpha1, np - 1)
end

research_labor_start = clamp.(
    diff(alpha_target_start) ./ alpha_bar,
    0.0,
    0.9 * omega,
)

    alpha1 .+
    alpha_bar .* vcat(
        0.0,
        cumsum(research_labor_start),

production_labor_start =
    vcat(
        omega .- research_labor_start,
        omega,
    )

The basic mechanism of the model is closely related to the R&D-based growth literature. Romer (1990) treats technological change as the outcome of intentional R&D investment and emphasizes the allocation of productive resources to research, while Jones (1995) considers a more general knowledge-production process in which the creation of new knowledge may depend on both R&D inputs and the existing stock of knowledge. The linear additive R&D specification adopted here can be viewed as a simple special case in which the increment in the production-efficiency parameter is proportional to current R&D labor and independent of the existing level of technology.
Assume the following:

The economy has \(n_p\) periods. A firm operating in period \(t\) starts production at the beginning of the period and obtains its product at the end of period \(t\), or equivalently at the beginning of period \(t+1\). Hence there are \(n_p-1\) interperiod production activities. In general, an \(n_p\)-period model may contain \(n_p\) dated products, but in the present example the initial-period product supply and consumption are omitted. The product commodities are therefore \(product^{(2)},\ldots,product^{(n_p)}\).
The economy contains four types of dated commodities: products, labor, technology knowledge (i.e., production-efficiency parameters), and scale claims. Product firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), R&D firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), and there is one intertemporal consumer. Commodities dated at different periods are treated as different commodities.
The product firm operating in period \(t\) uses the production-efficiency parameter \(\alpha^{(t)}\) and production labor \(x^{(t)}\) to produce the product available in period \(t+1\) according to \(c^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}\). To represent this technology as a degree-one homogeneous production function, a scale claim \(c_s^{(t)}\) is introduced, giving

\[
g\left(\alpha^{(t)},x^{(t)},c_s^{(t)}\right)
=
\frac{\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}}{c_s^{(t)}}
\]
The product firm follows the marginal pricing principle.

The R&D firm operating in period \(t\) uses R&D labor \(\ell^{(t)}\) to increase production efficiency from period \(t+1\) onward. With R&D-efficiency parameter \(\bar\alpha>0\), one unit of R&D labor generates \(\bar\alpha\) units of each future production-efficiency parameter commodity (i.e., technology knowledge) within the production horizon. Hence \(\alpha^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}+\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), or equivalently

\[
\alpha^{(t)}
=
\alpha^{(1)}
+
\bar\alpha
\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\ell^{(s)},
\qquad
t=2,\ldots,n_p-1
\]

The consumer is endowed with \(\omega>0\) units of labor and one unit of the scale claim in each production period, together with \(\alpha^{(1)}\) units of each dated production-efficiency parameter commodity. Labor-market balance is \(x^{(t)}+\ell^{(t)}=\omega\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), while \(x^{(n_p-1)}=\omega\) because R&D in the last production period cannot affect production within the horizon.
The consumer consumes \(c^{(2)},\ldots,c^{(n_p)}\) and has intertemporal utility

\[
u
=
\sum_{t=2}^{n_p}\rho^t\ln c^{(t)},
\qquad
0<\rho<1
\]
For the infinite-horizon version of the model, the critical production-efficiency level for R&D is
\[
\alpha^*
=
\frac{\rho\bar\alpha\omega}{1-\rho}
\tag{1}\]
R&D is undertaken when \(\alpha^{(t)}<\alpha^*\) and ceases once the production-efficiency parameter reaches the critical level. In particular, if \(\alpha^{(1)}\geq\alpha^*\), there is no incentive to undertake R&D.
The finite horizon generates a terminal effect. R&D undertaken late in the horizon affects fewer future production periods, so the incentive to undertake R&D declines near the terminal period and eventually disappears.
For \(n_p=9\), \(\rho=0.8\), \(\alpha^{(1)}=0.01\), \(\bar\alpha=0.0001\), and \(\omega=100\), the equilibrium R&D-labor path is approximately \((43.02,33.09,23.10,10.99,0,0,0)\). The corresponding productivity increments \(\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}\) are approximately \((0.004302,0.003309,0.002310,0.001099,0,0,0)\). The resulting productivity path is
\[
\left(
\alpha^{(2)},\ldots,\alpha^{(8)}
\right)
=
\left(
0.01430,\,
0.01761,\,
0.01992,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102
\right)
\]
Thus positive R&D occurs only in the first four R&D periods.

        1.0e-12,
        2 * nt,

    multiplier_start=multiplier_start,

title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Knowledge Production
section: Finite-Horizon Equilibrium with Linear Multiplicative R&D
text:
Finite-Horizon Equilibrium with Linear Multiplicative R&D

Linear Multiplicative R&D
We now modify the model from the previous section by replacing its R&D function.
Consider the multiplicative technology-accumulation equation
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}
\right)
\]
where \(\ell^{(t)}\) denotes R&D labor in period \(t\). Production in period \(t\) generates the product available in period \(t+1\), so production takes place in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), while useful R&D activities take place only in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\). The production relation is
\[
c^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}
\]
with \(x^{(t)}=\omega-\ell^{(t)}\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\) and \(x^{(n_p-1)}=\omega\).


Analytical Solution
For the infinite-horizon model, positive R&D occurs when
\[
\rho(1+\bar\alpha\omega)>1
\]
When this condition holds, the optimal R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^*
=
\rho\omega
-
\frac{1-\rho}{\bar\alpha}
\]
The corresponding productivity path is
\[
\alpha^{(t)}
=
\alpha^{(1)}
\left[
\rho(1+\bar\alpha\omega)
\right]^{t-1},
\qquad
t=1,2,\ldots
\]
For the finite-horizon model, define
\[
q^{(t)}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n_p-t-1}\rho^k
=
\frac{1-\rho^{n_p-t}}{1-\rho},
\qquad
t=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
The optimal R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^{*(t)}
=
\begin{cases}
0,
&
\displaystyle
q^{(t)}
\leq
1+\frac{1}{\bar\alpha\omega}
\\[1em]
\displaystyle
\omega
-
\frac{1}{q^{(t)}}
\left(
\omega+\frac{1}{\bar\alpha}
\right),
&
\displaystyle
q^{(t)}
>
1+\frac{1}{\bar\alpha\omega}
\end{cases}
\]
Thus R&D eventually disappears as the terminal period approaches. When the long-run R&D condition holds, define
\[
k^*
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{
\ln\left(
\rho-\frac{1-\rho}{\bar\alpha\omega}
\right)
}{
\ln\rho
}
\right\rfloor
\]
Provided that \(n_p\geq k^*+2\), the last period with positive R&D is \(n_p-k^*-1\). During periods with positive R&D, productivity evolves according to
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\rho(1+\bar\alpha\omega)
\frac{q^{(t+1)}}{q^{(t)}}
\]
and remains constant thereafter.



GEMB Implementation of the Multiplicative R&D Model
The GEMB implementation contains six types of dated commodities: product, labor, technology stock, technology service, product scale claim, and research scale claim. There are three types of economic agents: production firms, R&D firms, and a representative consumer. In addition, a terminal technology agent is introduced as a technical device in the final production period.
Several commodity types are introduced specifically for implementing the model. In particular, the technology stock and the technology service used in current production are represented separately. The technology stock available at the beginning of period \(t\) has two roles. It provides the technology service used by the period-\(t\) production firm, and it also serves as the technological base from which the next-period technology stock is generated. Separating these two roles makes it possible to represent explicitly both the current productive use of technology and its intertemporal accumulation.
Two different scale-claim commodities are also introduced. The product scale claim, denoted by \(c_p^{(t)}\), is associated with the production technology, while the research scale claim, denoted by \(c_r^{(t)}\), is associated with the R&D technology. One unit of each corresponding scale claim is supplied in each relevant period, so market clearing gives \(c_p^{(t)}=1\) and \(c_r^{(t)}=1\). These commodities allow the two technologies to be represented in degree-one homogeneous form.
The period-\(t\) production firm uses technology service, labor, and the product scale claim to produce the product available in period \(t+1\). Its homogenized production function is
\[
g(a,x,c_p)
=
\frac{ax}{c_p}
\]
where \(a\) is the technology service and \(x\) is production labor. When \(c_p=1\), this reduces to the original production relation
\[
c^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}
\]
The production firm can therefore be represented directly by a standard production-function specification with marginal-pricing conditions.
The R&D firm requires a different treatment. Let \(a\), \(\ell\), and \(c_r\) denote its inputs of current technology stock, R&D labor, and research scale claim. The firm supplies \(a\) units of current technology service and produces the next-period technology stock according to
\[
a'
=
a
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\frac{\ell}{c_r}
\right)
\]
This technology is homogeneous of degree one in \((a,\ell,c_r)\). When \(c_r=1\), it becomes
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}
\right)
\]
and hence
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}-\alpha^{(t)}
=
\bar\alpha\alpha^{(t)}\ell^{(t)}
\]
The productivity of R&D labor depends on the current technology stock, so one unit of R&D labor does not generate a fixed amount of future technology. The R&D firm cannot therefore be represented directly by an activity-demand specification.
The R&D firm also cannot be represented directly by the standard production-function specification. Although this specification allows joint outputs, their quantities are proportional to a common activity level through fixed output coefficients.
The R&D firm is consequently implemented as an explicit net-supply agent. Over current technology stock, labor, research scale claim, current technology service, and next-period technology stock, its net-supply vector is
\[
\bar{\mathbf s}
=
\left(
-a,\,
-\ell,\,
-c_r,\,
a,\,
a\left(1+\bar\alpha\frac{\ell}{c_r}\right)
\right)^\top
\]
The first three components are demands for current technology stock, labor, and the research scale claim, while the last two components are supplies of current technology service and next-period technology stock. The current technology stock is thus used both to provide current productive services and as the base for future technology accumulation.
Let \(p_a^{(t)}\), \(w^{(t)}\), \(p_r^{(t)}\), \(p_v^{(t)}\), and \(p_a^{(t+1)}\) denote the prices of current technology stock, labor, research scale claim, current technology service, and next-period technology stock, respectively. The corresponding explicit marginal-pricing conditions are
\[
w^{(t)}
=
p_a^{(t+1)}
\bar\alpha
\frac{a}{c_r}
\]
\[
p_a^{(t)}
=
p_v^{(t)}
+
p_a^{(t+1)}
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\frac{\ell}{c_r}
\right)
\]
and
\[
p_r^{(t)}
=
-
p_a^{(t+1)}
\bar\alpha
\frac{a\ell}{c_r^2}
\]
Although the R&D firm is associated with five commodities, only three marginal-pricing conditions are required because its independent decision variables are the three inputs \(a\), \(\ell\), and \(c_r\); the two outputs are determined by these inputs through the R&D technology.
The first condition equates the wage to the marginal value generated by an additional unit of R&D labor. The second decomposes the value of the current technology stock into the value of its current technology service and its contribution to the next-period technology stock. The third determines the price of the research scale claim associated with the degree-one homogenization. In the implementation, \(\ell\) is also used as the activity level of the R&D firm, so the reported R&D activity levels directly represent equilibrium R&D labor inputs.
The representative consumer supplies the dated labor endowments, the initial technology stock, and the scale-claim commodities, and demands the dated products. Since the consumer side is unchanged from the underlying intertemporal model, no additional behavioral specification is required for the multiplicative R&D mechanism.
Finally, there is no useful R&D activity in period \(n_p-1\), because technology generated in that period would become available only as \(\alpha^{(n_p)}\) and could not be used by any production activity within the finite horizon. A terminal technology agent is therefore introduced to convert the remaining technology stock into the technology service required by the final production firm. This terminal agent is a computational transfer device rather than an additional behavioral type of economic agent.


Numerical Equilibrium
The GEMB implementation described above can be illustrated with \(n_p=20\), \(\rho=0.7\), \(\alpha^{(1)}=1\), \(\bar\alpha=0.005\), and \(\omega=100\). For these parameters,
\[
\bar\alpha\omega=0.5>\frac{1}{\rho}-1
\]
so the corresponding infinite-horizon model has positive R&D. For the finite-horizon model, the analytical solution gives \(k^*=6\), implying that the last period with positive R&D is
\[
n_p-k^*-1=13
\]
Thus R&D is positive in periods \(1,\ldots,13\) and zero thereafter. Productivity increases through \(\alpha^{(14)}\) and then remains constant.
The numerical equilibrium obtained with GEMB reproduces these analytical results. In particular, the equilibrium R&D labor inputs coincide with the finite-horizon solution, and the resulting productivity path follows the corresponding technology-accumulation path. This provides a numerical verification of both the analytical solution and the GEMB representation of the multiplicative R&D technology.



Listing 3: A \(6\times3\) Technology-Accumulation Intertemporal Equilibrium Model with Linear Multiplicative R&D


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
import GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEM

np = 20

rho = 0.7
alpha1 = 1.0
alpha_bar = 0.005
omega = 100.0

np >= 3 || throw(ArgumentError("np must be at least 3."))

product(t) = CommodityRef(:product; period=t)
labor(t) = CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)
technology_stock(t) = CommodityRef(:technology_stock; period=t)
technology_service(t) = CommodityRef(:technology_service; period=t)
product_scale_claim(t) = CommodityRef(:product_scale_claim; period=t)
research_scale_claim(t) = CommodityRef(:research_scale_claim; period=t)

quantity_start = 100.0
research_start = 10.0

product_p0 =
    rho .^ (0:(np - 2))

labor_p0 =
    alpha1 .* product_p0

technology_service_p0 =
    quantity_start .* product_p0

technology_stock_p0 =
    copy(technology_service_p0)

for t in (np - 2):-1:1
    technology_stock_p0[t] =
        technology_service_p0[t] +
        (1 + alpha_bar * research_start) *
        technology_stock_p0[t + 1]
end

product_scale_claim_p0 =
    -quantity_start .* product_p0

research_scale_claim_p0 =
    -research_start .* alpha_bar .* technology_stock_p0[2:end]

p0 = vcat(
    product_p0,
    labor_p0,
    technology_stock_p0,
    technology_service_p0,
    product_scale_claim_p0,
    research_scale_claim_p0,
)

production_function =
    v -> v[1] * v[2] / v[3]

marginal_product_function = v -> begin
    a, x, cs = v
    [x * cs, a * cs, -a * x]
end

production_spec = ProductionFunctionSpec(
    production_function,
    marginal_product_function;
    behavior=:stationary,
)

research_net_supply = function (
    variables,
    prices,
    observed_values=Any[],
)
    ell, a, cs = variables
    [
        -a,
        -ell,
        -cs,
        a,
        a * (1 + alpha_bar * ell / cs),
    ]
end

research_conditions = function (
    variables,
    prices,
    net_supply,
)
    ell, a, cs = variables
    p_stock,
    wage,
    p_claim,
    p_service,
    p_next_stock = prices

    [
        wage -
        p_next_stock * alpha_bar * a / cs,

        p_stock -
        p_service -
        p_next_stock *
        (1 + alpha_bar * ell / cs),

        p_claim +
        p_next_stock *
        alpha_bar * a * ell / cs^2,
    ]
end

model = GEMBModel(
    [
        CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=2:np,),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :technology_stock;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :technology_service;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :product_scale_claim;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=-Inf,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :research_scale_claim;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 2),),
            price_lower_bound=-Inf,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=product(2),
)

for t in 1:(np - 1)
    add_agent!(
        model,
        production_spec;
        outputs=product(t + 1),
        demands=[
            technology_service(t),
            labor(t),
            product_scale_claim(t),
        ],
        activity_start=quantity_start,
        demand_start=[
            alpha1,
            quantity_start,
            1.0,
        ],
        demand_lower_bounds=fill(1.0e-12, 3),
        production_multiplier_start=product_p0[t],
        name=Symbol("production_$t"),
    )
end

for t in 1:(np - 2)
    add_net_supply_agent!(
        model,
        research_net_supply;
        commodities=[
            technology_stock(t),
            labor(t),
            research_scale_claim(t),
            technology_service(t),
            technology_stock(t + 1),
        ],
        variable_names=[
            :activity,
            :technology_input,
            :scale_claim,
        ],
        variable_lower_bounds=[
            0.0,
            1.0e-12,
            1.0e-12,
        ],
        variable_upper_bounds=[
            omega,
            Inf,
            Inf,
        ],
        variable_start=[
            research_start,
            alpha1,
            1.0,
        ],
        condition_rule=
            GEM.ExplicitAgentConditions(
                research_conditions,
            ),
        name=Symbol("research_$t"),
    )
end

add_agent!(
    model,
    ActivityDemandSpec(
        (activity, prices) -> [activity],
    );
    outputs=technology_service(np - 1),
    demands=technology_stock(np - 1),
    activity_start=alpha1,
    activity_lower_bound=0.0,
    name=:terminal_technology,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    CESMarginalUtilitySpec(
        rho .^ (2:np);
        es=1.0,
    );
    demands=[CommodityRef(:product)],
    endowments=[
        CommodityRef(:labor),
        technology_stock(1),
        CommodityRef(:product_scale_claim),
        CommodityRef(:research_scale_claim),
    ],
    endowment_quantities=vcat(
        fill(omega, np - 1),
        [alpha1],
        fill(1.0, np - 1),
        fill(1.0, np - 2),
    ),
    demand_start=fill(quantity_start, np - 1),
    demand_lower_bounds=fill(1.0e-12, np - 1),
    multiplier_start=
        rho^2 / quantity_start,
    multiplier_lower_bound=0.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

result = solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

stats = equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

print_equilibrium_statistics(
    model,
    result;
    show_matrices=false,
)

research_labor =
    stats.activity_levels[np:(2 * np - 3)]

alpha_path =
    alpha1 .* cumprod(
        1 .+ alpha_bar .* research_labor,
    )

text:
Exponential Multiplicative R&D
Consider an alternative multiplicative R&D specification,
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
e^{\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}}
\]
where \(\ell^{(t)}\) denotes R&D labor in period \(t\). As before, production in period \(t\) generates the product available in period \(t+1\), so useful R&D activities occur only in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\).

\[
\bar\alpha\omega
>
\frac{1}{\rho}-1
\]
and the corresponding R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^*
=
\omega
-
\frac{1-\rho}{\rho\bar\alpha}
\]
When R&D is positive, productivity follows
\[
\alpha^{(t)}
=
\alpha^{(1)}
\left(
e^{\bar\alpha\omega-\frac{1-\rho}{\rho}}
\right)^{t-1},
\qquad
t=1,2,\ldots
\]
For the finite-horizon model, the optimal R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^{*(t)}
=
\begin{cases}
0,
&
\displaystyle
\bar\alpha\omega
\leq
\frac{1-\rho}
{\rho\left(1-\rho^{n_p-t-1}\right)}
\\[1em]
\displaystyle
\omega
-
\frac{1-\rho}
{\rho\bar\alpha\left(1-\rho^{n_p-t-1}\right)},
&
\displaystyle
\bar\alpha\omega
>
\frac{1-\rho}
{\rho\left(1-\rho^{n_p-t-1}\right)}
\end{cases},
\qquad
t=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]

\[

=
\left\lfloor
\frac{

1-\frac{1-\rho}{\rho\bar\alpha\omega}
\right)
}{
\ln\rho

\right\rfloor
+1
\]

title: Endogenous Interest Rates and Capital Accumulation
text:
This example extends the preceding intertemporal equilibrium model by introducing endogenous capital accumulation and Cobb–Douglas production. Product retained by the firm in one period becomes capital in the next period and is completely exhausted in production. Initial capital, however, is owned by the consumer and must be purchased by the firm. Thus, the purchase of initial capital requires money, whereas subsequent capital accumulation is an internal transfer within the intertemporal firm and does not require a monetary transaction.
The model contains three types of dated commodities, namely product, labor, and money, and two types of economic agents, namely a firm and a consumer.
Assume the following:

The economy operates for \(n_p\geq3\) periods. Production takes place in periods \(i=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), so there are \(n_p-1\) production activities.
The consumer initially owns \(\bar k>0\) units of product 1, which are purchased by the firm and used as capital in period 1. The consumer also supplies \(\omega^{(i)}>0\) units of labor in production period \(i\), \(i=1,\ldots,n_p-1\).
Production in period \(i\) is described by the constant-returns-to-scale Cobb–Douglas production function

\[
y^{(i)}
=
\alpha^{(i)} \left(k^{(i)}\right)^{\theta} \left(l^{(i)}\right)^{1-\theta},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1,
\qquad
\alpha^{(i)}>0,
\qquad
0<\theta<1
\]
where \(k^{(i)}\) and \(l^{(i)}\) denote capital and labor inputs. Period-\(i\) production yields product \(i+1\). Capital is completely exhausted in production.

The initial capital stock satisfies

\[
k^{(1)}=\bar k
\]
For \(i=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), period-\(i\) output is divided between consumption in period \(i+1\) and capital carried internally into the next production period:
\[
y^{(i)}=c^{(i+1)}+k^{(i+1)}
\]
In the terminal production period,
\[
y^{(n_p-1)}=c^{(n_p)}
\]

The purchase of initial capital and labor in period 1 requires money. From period 2 onward, capital is carried internally by the firm and therefore does not require a monetary transaction. The purchase of labor continues to require money in every production period.
The consumer has Cobb–Douglas preferences over dated consumption and terminal money holdings:

\[
u
=
\left(
\prod_{t=2}^{n_p}\left(c^{(t)}\right)^{\beta^{(t)}}
\right)
\left(h^{(n_p)}\right)^{\beta_m}
\]
where
\[
\beta^{(2)}>\beta^{(3)}>\cdots>\beta^{(n_p)}>\beta_m>0,
\qquad
\sum_{t=2}^{n_p}\beta^{(t)}+\beta_m=1
\]

The consumer is endowed with one unit of each dated money commodity, from money 1 through money \(n_p\). Let \(p_m^{(i)}\) denote the price of money in period \(i\). Money \(n_p\) is terminal money. The interest rate in production period \(i\) is

\[
r^{(i)}
=
\frac{
p_m^{(i)}
}{
\displaystyle\sum_{j=i+1}^{n_p}p_m^{(j)}
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
A positive terminal money value therefore keeps all production-period interest rates finite.
Let \(p^{(t)}\) denote the price of product \(t\), \(t=1,\ldots,n_p\), and let \(p_l^{(i)}\) denote the price of labor in production period \(i\).

title: Endogenous Interest Rates and Capital Accumulation
text:
Analytical Solution

Production and Monetary Transactions
Under Cobb–Douglas production, the production stationarity conditions imply the value-share relations
\[
(1+r^{(1)})p^{(1)}k^{(1)}=\theta p^{(2)}y^{(1)},
\qquad
(1+r^{(1)})p_l^{(1)}l^{(1)}=(1-\theta)p^{(2)}y^{(1)}
\]
in period 1. Since both initial capital and labor are purchased from the consumer, the firm’s money holdings satisfy
\[
p_m^{(1)}h_f^{(1)}
=
\frac{r^{(1)}}{1+r^{(1)}}p^{(2)}y^{(1)}
\]
From period 2 onward, capital is carried internally from the firm’s previous-period output rather than purchased through a market transaction. The corresponding value-share relations are
\[
p^{(i)} k^{(i)}=\theta p^{(i+1)}y^{(i)},
\qquad
(1+r^{(i)})p_l^{(i)}l^{(i)}=(1-\theta)p^{(i+1)}y^{(i)},
\qquad
i=2,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
Only labor purchases require money in these periods, so
\[
p_m^{(i)}h_f^{(i)}
=
\frac{r^{(i)}}{1+r^{(i)}}(1-\theta)p^{(i+1)}y^{(i)},
\qquad
i=2,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
Thus, the first production period differs from subsequent periods because the initial capital stock is purchased from the consumer, whereas later capital is accumulated and carried internally by the firm.


Consumer Demand and Money-Market Clearing
Let \(w\) denote consumer income, equal to the value of the initial capital, labor, and money endowments:
\[
w=p^{(1)}\bar k+\sum_{i=1}^{n_p-1}p_l^{(i)}\omega^{(i)}+\sum_{i=1}^{n_p}p_m^{(i)}
\]
For production period \(i\), the consumer’s demand for product \(i+1\) and the associated money holdings are
\[
c^{(i+1)}
=
\frac{\beta^{(i+1)}w}{(1+r^{(i)})p^{(i+1)}},
\qquad
p_m^{(i)}h_c^{(i)}
=
\frac{r^{(i)}\beta^{(i+1)}w}{1+r^{(i)}},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
Terminal money holdings satisfy
\[
h^{(n_p)}
=
\frac{\beta_m w}{p_m^{(n_p)}}
\]
and, since the terminal money supply is one,
\[
p_m^{(n_p)}
=
\beta_m w
\]
Money-market clearing therefore gives
\[
p_m^{(1)}
=
\frac{r^{(1)}}{1+r^{(1)}}
\left(
p^{(2)}y^{(1)}+\beta^{(2)}w
\right)
\]
for period 1, and
\[
p_m^{(i)}
=
\frac{r^{(i)}}{1+r^{(i)}}
\left[
(1-\theta)p^{(i+1)}y^{(i)}+\beta^{(i+1)}w
\right],
\qquad
i=2,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
for subsequent production periods. The difference again reflects that only the initial capital purchase requires money.


Recursive Analytical Solution for the Interest Rates
Define the tail value of money prices by
\[
v^{(i)}
:=
\sum_{j=i}^{n_p}p_m^{(j)}
\]
and normalize it by consumer income:
\[
g^{(i)}
:=
\frac{v^{(i)}}{w}
\]
The terminal condition is
\[
g^{(n_p)}=\beta_m
\]
From the definition of the interest rate,
\[
p_m^{(i)}
=
r^{(i)}v^{(i+1)}
\]
and
\[
v^{(i)}
=
(1+r^{(i)})v^{(i+1)}
\]
Hence,
\[
1+r^{(i)}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}
\]
and the equilibrium interest rates are
\[
r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}-1,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
Moreover,
\[
\frac{p_m^{(i)}}{w}
=
g^{(i)}-g^{(i+1)}
\]
and
\[
\frac{r^{(i)}}{1+r^{(i)}}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}-g^{(i+1)}}{g^{(i)}}
\]
For the strictly positive interest-rate solution, whose positivity is established below, \(g^{(i)}-g^{(i+1)}>0\). Cancelling this factor in the period-1 money-market condition gives
\[
\frac{p^{(2)}y^{(1)}}{w}
=
g^{(1)}-\beta^{(2)}
\]
For periods \(i=2,\ldots,n_p-1\), money-market clearing gives
\[
\frac{p^{(i+1)}y^{(i)}}{w}
=
\frac{
g^{(i)}-\beta^{(i+1)}
}{
1-\theta
}
\]
These relations allow the interest-rate system to be solved independently of the levels of output and prices.
In the terminal production period,
\[
y^{(n_p-1)}=c^{(n_p)}
\]
and therefore
\[
\frac{
g^{(n_p-1)}-\beta^{(n_p)}
}{
1-\theta
}
=
\beta^{(n_p)}
\frac{
g^{(n_p)}
}{
g^{(n_p-1)}
}
\]
Thus,
\[
\left(g^{(n_p-1)}\right)^{2}
-
\beta^{(n_p)}g^{(n_p-1)}
-
(1-\theta)\beta^{(n_p)}g^{(n_p)}
=
0
\]
and the positive solution is
\[
g^{(n_p-1)}
=
\frac{
\beta^{(n_p)}
+
\sqrt{
\left(\beta^{(n_p)}\right)^{2}
+
4(1-\theta)\beta^{(n_p)}g^{(n_p)}
}
}{
2
}
\]
For a nonterminal production period \(i\), the value of the product internally retained as next-period capital is determined by the capital value-share relation for period \(i+1\):
\[
p^{(i+1)}k^{(i+1)}
=
\theta p^{(i+2)}y^{(i+1)}
\]
Hence,
\[
\frac{
p^{(i+1)}k^{(i+1)}
}{
w
}
=
\frac{
\theta
}{
1-\theta
}
\left(
g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)}
\right)
\]
For periods \(i=2,\ldots,n_p-2\), product allocation requires
\[
p^{(i+1)}y^{(i)}
=
p^{(i+1)}c^{(i+1)}+p^{(i+1)}k^{(i+1)}
\]
Using the preceding relations gives
\[
\frac{
g^{(i)}-\beta^{(i+1)}
}{
1-\theta
}
=
\beta^{(i+1)}
\frac{
g^{(i+1)}
}{
g^{(i)}
}
+
\frac{
\theta
}{
1-\theta
}
\left(
g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)}
\right)
\]
Define
\[
d^{(i)}
:=
\theta
\left(
g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)}
\right),
\qquad
i=2,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
Then
\[
\left(g^{(i)}\right)^{2}
-
(\beta^{(i+1)}+d^{(i)})g^{(i)}
-
(1-\theta)\beta^{(i+1)}g^{(i+1)}
=
0
\]
and therefore
\[
g^{(i)}
=
\frac{
\beta^{(i+1)}+d^{(i)}
+
\sqrt{
(\beta^{(i+1)}+d^{(i)})^2
+
4(1-\theta)\beta^{(i+1)}g^{(i+1)}
}
}{
2
}
\]
The first production period differs because the purchase of initial capital requires money. Product-market clearing still gives
\[
p^{(2)}y^{(1)}
=
p^{(2)}c^{(2)}+p^{(2)}k^{(2)}
\]
but
\[
\frac{p^{(2)}y^{(1)}}{w}
=
g^{(1)}-\beta^{(2)}
\]
rather than the corresponding expression divided by \(1-\theta\). Define
\[
d^{(1)}
:=
\frac{
\theta
}{
1-\theta
}
\left(
g^{(2)}-\beta^{(3)}
\right)
\]
Then
\[
\left(g^{(1)}\right)^{2}
-
(\beta^{(2)}+d^{(1)})g^{(1)}
-
\beta^{(2)}g^{(2)}
=
0
\]
and
\[
g^{(1)}
=
\frac{
\beta^{(2)}+d^{(1)}
+
\sqrt{
(\beta^{(2)}+d^{(1)})^2
+
4\beta^{(2)}g^{(2)}
}
}{
2
}
\]
The complete analytical solution can therefore be obtained by backward recursion. Starting from
\[
g^{(n_p)}=\beta_m
\]
one first obtains \(g^{(n_p-1)}\), then successively computes
\[
g^{(n_p-2)},
\ldots,
g^{(2)}
\]
using the common intermediate-period recursion, and finally computes \(g^{(1)}\) using the first-period formula.
The equilibrium interest rates then follow from
\[
r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}-1,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
The decreasing-share assumption guarantees that all the resulting interest rates are strictly positive. At the terminal step, \(g^{(n_p)}=\beta_m<\beta^{(n_p)}\), and the terminal quadratic gives
\[
\max\{g^{(n_p)},\beta^{(n_p)}\}<g^{(n_p-1)}<2\beta^{(n_p)}
\]
For an intermediate period, define
\[
P^{(i)}(x)=x^2-[\beta^{(i+1)}+\theta(g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)})]x-(1-\theta)\beta^{(i+1)}g^{(i+1)}
\]
Suppose \(\beta^{(i+2)}<g^{(i+1)}<2\beta^{(i+2)}\). Since \(\beta^{(i+1)}>\beta^{(i+2)}\), direct substitution gives \(P^{(i)}(g^{(i+1)})<0\), \(P^{(i)}(\beta^{(i+1)})<0\), and \(P^{(i)}(2\beta^{(i+1)})>0\). Its positive root therefore satisfies
\[
\max\{g^{(i+1)},\beta^{(i+1)}\}<g^{(i)}<2\beta^{(i+1)}
\]
This proves the intermediate steps by backward induction. For period 1, the coefficient \(d^{(1)}\) and the magnitude of the constant term in its quadratic are strictly larger than those obtained by applying the intermediate-period formula at \(i=1\). Its positive root is consequently larger as well, so \(g^{(1)}>g^{(2)}\). Thus,
\[
g^{(1)}>g^{(2)}>\cdots>g^{(n_p)}>0
\]
and \(r^{(i)*}>0\) for every production period. This also validates the cancellation used to obtain the recursion.
Thus, despite the distinction between externally purchased initial capital and internally accumulated subsequent capital, the model retains an analytical backward-recursive solution.
An important feature of the solution is that
\[
r^{(i)*}
=
r^{(i)*}
\left(
\boldsymbol\beta,
\beta_m,
\theta
\right)
\]
The productivity parameters \(\alpha^{(i)}\), the labor endowments \(\omega^{(i)}\), and the initial capital endowment \(\bar k\) do not enter the normalized interest-rate recursion directly. They determine the equilibrium quantities and price levels once the interest rates have been obtained.


Capital and Output Paths
After solving for the \(g^{(i)}\), the capital path can also be obtained recursively. Labor-market clearing gives
\[
l^{(i)*}=\omega^{(i)},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-1
\]
and production is
\[
y^{(i)*}
=
\alpha^{(i)}
(k^{(i)*})^\theta
\left(\omega^{(i)}\right)^{1-\theta}
\]
For the first production period, the share of output retained as capital is
\[
s^{(1)*}
=
\frac{
\theta
\left(
g^{(2)}-\beta^{(3)}
\right)
}{
(1-\theta)
\left(
g^{(1)}-\beta^{(2)}
\right)
}
\]
For periods \(i=2,\ldots,n_p-2\),
\[
s^{(i)*}
=
\frac{
\theta
\left(
g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)}
\right)
}{
g^{(i)}-\beta^{(i+1)}
}
\]
Therefore,
\[
k^{(i+1)*}
=
s^{(i)*}y^{(i)*},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
Starting from
\[
k^{(1)*}=\bar k
\]
the entire sequence of capital, output, and consumption can be determined recursively.


Vanishing Terminal Money Value
The role of terminal money can be examined by letting
\[
\beta_m\rightarrow0^+
\]
while maintaining the relative proportions of the consumption shares. More precisely, write \(\beta^{(t)}=(1-\varepsilon)b^{(t)}\), where \(\varepsilon=\beta_m\), \(b^{(2)}>\cdots>b^{(n_p)}>0\), and \(\sum_{t=2}^{n_p}b^{(t)}=1\). The maintained decreasing-share assumption holds for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\).
Since
\[
g^{(n_p)}=\beta_m
\]
the terminal recursion implies
\[
g^{(n_p-1)}
\rightarrow
\beta^{(n_p)}
\]
More precisely, if \(\beta_m=\varepsilon\), then
\[
g^{(n_p-1)}
=
\beta^{(n_p)}
+
(1-\theta)\varepsilon
+
O(\varepsilon^2)
\]
The terminal production-period interest rate therefore satisfies
\[
r^{(n_p-1)*}
=
\frac{
g^{(n_p-1)}
}{
\beta_m
}
-1
\rightarrow+\infty
\]
At the same time, the value of capital carried into the terminal production period is
\[
\frac{
p^{(n_p-1)}k^{(n_p-1)}
}{
w
}
=
\frac{
\theta
}{
1-\theta
}
\left(
g^{(n_p-1)}-\beta^{(n_p)}
\right)
\]
and therefore
\[
\frac{
p^{(n_p-1)}k^{(n_p-1)}
}{
w
}
\rightarrow0
\]
To obtain the corresponding quantity limit, use the investment-share recursion. For \(n_p\geq4\),
\[
s^{(n_p-2)*}=
\frac{\theta(g^{(n_p-1)}-\beta^{(n_p)})}
{g^{(n_p-2)}-\beta^{(n_p-1)}}
\rightarrow0
\]
The numerator tends to zero, whereas the denominator has a strictly positive limit: the preceding quadratic retains a strictly negative constant term in the limit. For \(n_p=3\), the first-period investment-share formula gives the same conclusion. Earlier output remains bounded because the horizon and production parameters are fixed and each investment share lies between zero and one. Hence,
\[
k^{(n_p-1)*}=s^{(n_p-2)*}y^{(n_p-2)*}\rightarrow0
\]
and the terminal production function implies
\[
y^{(n_p-1)*}\rightarrow0
\]
Since all terminal output is consumed,
\[
c^{(n_p)*}\rightarrow0
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
\frac{\partial y^{(n_p-1)}}{\partial k^{(n_p-1)}}
=
\theta\alpha^{(n_p-1)}
\left(k^{(n_p-1)}\right)^{\theta-1}
\left(\omega^{(n_p-1)}\right)^{1-\theta}
\rightarrow+\infty
\]
Thus, as the terminal money value approaches zero,
\[
r^{(n_p-1)*}\rightarrow+\infty,
\qquad
k^{(n_p-1)*}\rightarrow0,
\qquad
y^{(n_p-1)*}\rightarrow0,
\qquad
c^{(n_p)*}\rightarrow0
\]
This is a terminal effect rather than a collapse of the entire economy. Production, consumption, and capital accumulation in earlier periods can remain positive and well defined. The vanishing terminal money value eliminates investment into the final production period, causing economic activity only in that final production period to approach zero.


Numerical Example
Consider a four-period economy with
\[
n_p=4
\]
and therefore three production periods. Let the capital share be
\[
\theta=\frac12
\]
The production functions are
\[
y^{(i)}=\left(k^{(i)}\right)^{1/2}\left(l^{(i)}\right)^{1/2},
\qquad
i=1,2,3
\]
so that
\[
\alpha^{(1)}=\alpha^{(2)}=\alpha^{(3)}=1
\]
The consumer initially owns
\[
\bar k=62
\]
units of product 1 and supplies labor endowments
\[
(\omega^{(1)},\omega^{(2)},\omega^{(3)})
=
(62,32,20)
\]
The supply of each dated money commodity, from money 1 through money 4, is one unit.
Let the Cobb–Douglas shares for consumption and terminal money holdings be
\[
(\beta^{(2)},\beta^{(3)},\beta^{(4)},\beta_m)
=
\frac1{775}
(352,228,120,75)
\]
so that
\[
\beta^{(2)}+\beta^{(3)}+\beta^{(4)}+\beta_m=1
\]
where \(\beta_m\) is the share for terminal money holdings. Product 2 is the numeraire.
Using the backward recursion, the normalized tail values of money prices are
\[
(g^{(1)},g^{(2)},g^{(3)},g^{(4)})
=
\left(
\frac{24}{31},
\frac{12}{31},
\frac6{31},
\frac3{31}
\right)
\]
Therefore,
\[
r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}-1
\]
gives
\[
r^{(1)*}=r^{(2)*}=r^{(3)*}=1
\]
The consumer’s equilibrium income is
\[
w^*
=
\frac{775}{4}
=
193.75
\]
The equilibrium capital stocks are
\[
(k^{(1)*},k^{(2)*},k^{(3)*})
=
(62,18,5)
\]
and the corresponding outputs are
\[
(y^{(1)*},y^{(2)*},y^{(3)*})
=
(62,24,10)
\]
Hence, product consumption is
\[
(c^{(2)*},c^{(3)*},c^{(4)*})
=
(44,19,10)
\]
Indeed,
\[
62=44+18
\]
and
\[
24=19+5
\]
while terminal consumption equals the terminal output of 10 units.
The investment shares are therefore
\[
s^{(1)*}
=
\frac{18}{62}
=
\frac9{31}
\]
and
\[
s^{(2)*}
=
\frac5{24}
\]
The equilibrium product prices are
\[
(p^{(1)*},p^{(2)*},p^{(3)*},p^{(4)*})
=
\left(
\frac14,
1,
\frac32,
\frac32
\right)
\]
and the labor prices are
\[
(p_l^{(1)*},p_l^{(2)*},p_l^{(3)*})
=
\left(
\frac14,
\frac9{32},
\frac3{16}
\right)
\]
The equilibrium money prices are
\[
(p_m^{(1)*},p_m^{(2)*},p_m^{(3)*},p_m^{(4)*})
=
\left(
75,
\frac{75}{2},
\frac{75}{4},
\frac{75}{4}
\right)
\]
These prices are consistent with the tail money values
\[
v^{(i)*}
=
\sum_{j=i}^4p_m^{(j)*}
\]
and
\[
g^{(i)}
=
\frac{v^{(i)*}}{w^*}
\]
For example,
\[
v^{(1)*}=150,
\qquad
v^{(2)*}=75,
\qquad
v^{(3)*}=\frac{75}{2},
\qquad
v^{(4)*}=\frac{75}{4}
\]
so that
\[
\frac{v^{(1)*}}{v^{(2)*}}
=
\frac{v^{(2)*}}{v^{(3)*}}
=
\frac{v^{(3)*}}{v^{(4)*}}
=
2
\]
which again implies
\[
r^{(1)*}=r^{(2)*}=r^{(3)*}=1
\]
The first-period firm purchases both initial capital and labor from the consumer. Its expenditure is
\[
p^{(1)*}k^{(1)*}
+
p_l^{(1)*}l^{(1)*}
=
\frac14(62)+\frac14(62)
=
31
\]
Since \(r^{(1)*}=1\), its period-1 money holdings are
\[
h_f^{(1)*}
=
\frac{31}{75}
\]
The consumer’s period-1 money holdings are
\[
h_c^{(1)*}
=
\frac{44}{75}
\]
and therefore
\[
h_f^{(1)*}+h_c^{(1)*}=1
\]
From period 2 onward, capital is carried internally by the firm and does not require a monetary transaction. Only labor purchases generate the firm’s money demand. The firm and consumer money holdings are
\[
(h_f^{(2)*},h_c^{(2)*})
=
\left(
\frac6{25},
\frac{19}{25}
\right)
\]
and
\[
(h_f^{(3)*},h_c^{(3)*})
=
\left(
\frac15,
\frac45
\right)
\]
so that each production-period money market clears:
\[
h_f^{(i)*}+h_c^{(i)*}=1,
\qquad
i=1,2,3
\]
Finally, the consumer holds the entire unit of terminal money:
\[
h^{(4)*}=1
\]
Thus, this numerical example gives a particularly simple equilibrium in which all three endogenous interest rates equal one, while capital accumulation, production, consumption, and sequential monetary transactions remain nontrivial.



Listing 1: A \(3\times2\) Intertemporal Equilibrium Model with Endogenous Interest Rates and Capital Accumulation


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEM
using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB

# Parameters
n_p = 4
n_prod = n_p - 1

theta = 0.5
alpha = ones(n_prod)

initial_capital = 62.0
omega = [62.0, 32.0, 20.0]

# Consumption shares for products 2,...,n_p
beta = [352.0, 228.0, 120.0] ./ 775.0

# Share spent on terminal money in period n_p
beta_terminal_money = 75.0 / 775.0

@assert isapprox(
    sum(beta) + beta_terminal_money,
    1.0;
    atol=1e-12,
)

# Commodities
model = GEMBModel(
    [
        CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=1:n_p,),
            price_lower_bound=1e-10,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:n_prod,),
            price_lower_bound=1e-10,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :money;
            axes=(period=1:n_p,),
            price_lower_bound=1e-10,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=CommodityRef(:product; period=2),
    numeraire_value=1.0,
)

# Endogenous interest rates
#
#     r_i = p_money_i / sum_{j=i+1}^{n_p} p_money_j,
#     i = 1,...,n_p-1
rate_names = [Symbol("r$i") for i in 1:n_prod]

add_agent!(
    model,
    ConditionAgentSpec(
        (r, p_m) -> [
            r[i] - p_m[i] / sum(p_m[(i + 1):n_p])
            for i in 1:n_prod
        ],
    );
    variable_names=rate_names,
    variable_start=ones(n_prod),
    variable_lower_bounds=zeros(n_prod),
    variable_upper_bounds=Inf,
    observed_variables=[
        PriceVariableRef(Symbol("money_$i"))
        for i in 1:n_p
    ],
    name=:interestRateDeterminer,
)

rate_refs = [
    agent_variable_ref(:interestRateDeterminer, rate_names[i])
    for i in 1:n_prod
]

# Production activities of the intertemporal firm
#
#     y_i = alpha_i * k_i^theta * l_i^(1-theta)
#
# Period i uses product i as capital and produces product i+1.
#
# In period 1, both capital and labor are market purchases:
#
#     effective prices = [(1+r_1)p_1, (1+r_1)p_l1]
#
# From period 2 onward, capital is carried internally:
#
#     effective prices = [p_i, (1+r_i)p_li]
#
activity_start = [60.0, 25.0, 10.0]

for i in 1:n_prod
    firm = ActivityDemandSpec(
        (y, p, obs) -> begin
            p_k, p_l, p_m = p
            r = obs[1]

            effective_prices =
                i == 1 ?
                [(1.0 + r) * p_k, (1.0 + r) * p_l] :
                [p_k, (1.0 + r) * p_l]

            x = GEMB.CES_input(
                [theta, 1.0 - theta],
                y,
                effective_prices;
                es=1.0,
                alpha=alpha[i],
            )

            h_f =
                i == 1 ?
                r * (p_k * x[1] + p_l * x[2]) / p_m :
                r * p_l * x[2] / p_m

            [x[1], x[2], h_f]
        end,
    )

    add_agent!(
        model,
        firm;
        outputs=CommodityRef(:product; period=i + 1),
        output_coefficients=1.0,
        demands=[
            CommodityRef(:product; period=i),
            CommodityRef(:labor; period=i),
            CommodityRef(:money; period=i),
        ],
        observed_variables=[rate_refs[i]],
        activity_start=activity_start[i],
        name=Symbol("firm$i"),
    )
end

# Consumer
product_refs = [
    CommodityRef(:product; period=i + 1)
    for i in 1:n_prod
]

labor_refs = [
    CommodityRef(:labor; period=i)
    for i in 1:n_prod
]

money_refs = [
    CommodityRef(:money; period=i)
    for i in 1:n_p
]

consumer = MarshallDemandConsumerSpec(
    (w, p, r) -> begin
        p_x = p[1:n_prod]
        p_m = p[(n_prod + 1):(n_prod + n_p)]

        c = [
            beta[i] * w /
            ((1.0 + r[i]) * p_x[i])
            for i in 1:n_prod
        ]

        h = [
            r[i] * beta[i] * w /
            ((1.0 + r[i]) * p_m[i])
            for i in 1:n_prod
        ]

        [
            c;
            h;
            beta_terminal_money * w / p_m[n_p];
        ]
    end,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    consumer;
    demands=[product_refs; money_refs],
    endowments=[
        CommodityRef(:product; period=1);
        labor_refs;
        money_refs;
    ],
    endowment_quantities=[
        initial_capital;
        omega;
        ones(n_p);
    ],
    observed_variables=rate_refs,
    name=:consumer,
)

# Starting prices
#
# product 1,...,4;
# labor 1,...,3;
# money 1,...,4
p0 = [
    0.30, 1.00, 1.40, 1.40,
    0.30, 0.30, 0.20,
    70.0, 35.0, 20.0, 20.0,
]

# Solve
result = solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1e-8,
    silent=true,
)

# Results
rates = result.agent_variable_values[1]

outputs = [
    result.agent_variable_values[i + 1][1]
    for i in 1:n_prod
]

p = result.prices

product_prices = p[1:n_p]
labor_prices = p[(n_p + 1):(n_p + n_prod)]
money_prices = p[(n_p + n_prod + 1):(2 * n_p + n_prod)]

w =
    product_prices[1] * initial_capital +
    sum(labor_prices .* omega) +
    sum(money_prices)

# Consumption of products 2,...,n_p
consumption = [
    beta[i] * w /
    ((1.0 + rates[i]) * product_prices[i + 1])
    for i in 1:n_prod
]

# Capital stocks k_1,...,k_{n_p-1}
capital = [
    initial_capital;
    [
        outputs[i] - consumption[i]
        for i in 1:(n_prod - 1)
    ];
]

println("Solved:          ", result.solved)
println("Periods:         ", n_p)
println("Production periods: ", n_prod)
println("Prices:          ", p)
println("Interest rates:  ", rates)

println("Consumption:     ", consumption)
println("Consumer income: ", w)

title: Endogenous Interest Rates and Capital Accumulation
text:
Infinite-Horizon Equilibrium
Consider an infinite-horizon version of the model, with production periods \(i=1,2,\ldots\). There is no terminal money commodity in utility and no terminal production condition. The consumer owns the initial capital stock and one unit of each dated money commodity, and supplies labor in each production period.
Let \(0<\rho<1\) and consider the geometric consumption shares
\[
\beta^{(t)}=(1-\rho)\rho^{t-2},
\qquad t=2,3,\ldots,
\qquad \sum_{t=2}^{\infty}\beta^{(t)}=1
\]
We construct an infinite-horizon equilibrium with finite income \(w>0\) and summable positive dated-money prices. Define
\[
v^{(i)}=\sum_{j=i}^{\infty}p_m^{(j)},
\qquad g^{(i)}=\frac{v^{(i)}}{w}
\]
The claim-rate relation remains \(1+r^{(i)}=g^{(i)}/g^{(i+1)}\). The construction below directly solves the infinite-horizon equations; it does not rely on a finite-horizon truncation with a terminal money preference weight.
For production periods \(i\geq2\), the production, product-allocation, and money-market equations give
\[
d^{(i)}
=
\theta
\left(
g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)}
\right)
\]
and
\[
\left(g^{(i)}\right)^{2}
-
(\beta^{(i+1)}+d^{(i)})g^{(i)}
-
(1-\theta)\beta^{(i+1)}g^{(i+1)}
=
0
\]
Equivalently, the positive-root recursion is
\[
g^{(i)}
=
\frac{
\beta^{(i+1)}
+
\theta(g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)})
+
\sqrt{
[\beta^{(i+1)}+\theta(g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)})]^2
+
4(1-\theta)\beta^{(i+1)}g^{(i+1)}
}
}{
2
}
\]
Because the preference weights are geometric, consider a stationary proportional solution of the form
\[
g^{(i)}=C\beta^{(i+1)},
\qquad
i\geq2
\]
Since
\[
\beta^{(i+2)}=\rho\beta^{(i+1)}
\]
we have
\[
g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)}
=
\rho\beta^{(i+1)}(C-1)
\]
Substituting these expressions into the recursive equation gives
\[
C
=
\frac{
1+\rho-2\theta\rho
}{
1-\theta\rho
}
\]
The equilibrium interest rate therefore satisfies
\[
1+r^{(i)*}
=
\frac{g^{(i)}}{g^{(i+1)}}
=
\frac1{\rho}
\]
and hence
\[
r^{(i)*}
=
\frac1{\rho}-1,
\qquad
i\geq2
\]
Thus, away from the initial period, the infinite-horizon economy admits a constant equilibrium interest rate determined by the intertemporal discount factor.
Here \(C-1=\rho(1-\theta)/(1-\theta\rho)>0\). The implied money prices are
\[
p_m^{(i)}=w(g^{(i)}-g^{(i+1)})=wC(1-\rho)\beta^{(i+1)},
\qquad i\geq2
\]
They are positive and summable, and satisfy
\[
\sum_{j=i}^{\infty}p_m^{(j)}=wC\beta^{(i+1)}=wg^{(i)},
\qquad i\geq2
\]
Thus the tail-value definition is satisfied and \(v^{(i)}\rightarrow0\) as \(i\rightarrow\infty\).
For the initial period, set \(g^{(2)}=C\beta^{(3)}\) and use the first-period formula
\[
d^{(1)}=\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}(g^{(2)}-\beta^{(3)}),
\qquad
g^{(1)}=\frac{\beta^{(2)}+d^{(1)}+\sqrt{(\beta^{(2)}+d^{(1)})^2+4\beta^{(2)}g^{(2)}}}{2}
\]
Since \(1<C<2\) and \(\beta^{(2)}>\beta^{(3)}\), the same root comparison as in the finite-horizon model gives \(g^{(1)}>g^{(2)}\). Consequently, \(r^{(1)*}=g^{(1)}/g^{(2)}-1>0\) and \(p_m^{(1)}=w(g^{(1)}-g^{(2)})>0\). The first-period investment share remains the one given in the capital-path subsection; the constant investment share derived below applies from period 2 onward.
The investment share also becomes constant. For \(i\geq2\),
\[
s^{(i)*}
=
\frac{
\theta(g^{(i+1)}-\beta^{(i+2)})
}{
g^{(i)}-\beta^{(i+1)}
}
\]
Using \(g^{(i)}=C\beta^{(i+1)}\) and \(\beta^{(i+2)}=\rho\beta^{(i+1)}\) gives
\[
s^{(i)*}
=
\theta\rho
\]
Hence, capital accumulation satisfies
\[
k^{(i+1)*}
=
\theta\rho y^{(i)*}
\]
With the Cobb–Douglas production function
\[
y^{(i)*}
=
\alpha^{(i)}
(k^{(i)*})^\theta
\left(\omega^{(i)}\right)^{1-\theta}
\]
the capital dynamics become
\[
k^{(i+1)*}
=
\theta\rho\alpha^{(i)}
(k^{(i)*})^\theta
\left(\omega^{(i)}\right)^{1-\theta}
\]
If productivity and labor endowment are constant over time,
\[
\alpha^{(i)}=\alpha
\]
and
\[
\omega^{(i)}=\omega
\]
the economy admits a steady state satisfying
\[
k^*
=
\theta\rho\alpha
(k^*)^\theta
\omega^{1-\theta}
\]
Therefore,
\[
k^*
=
\left(
\theta\rho\alpha
\omega^{1-\theta}
\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\theta}}
\]
Steady-state output is
\[
y^*
=
\alpha
(k^*)^\theta
\omega^{1-\theta}
\]
and steady-state consumption is
\[
c^*
=
(1-\theta\rho)y^*
\]
The corresponding steady-state interest rate and investment rate are
\[
r^*
=
\frac1{\rho}-1
\]
and
\[
s^*
=
\theta\rho
\]
respectively.
The first production period remains structurally different because the initial capital stock is owned by the consumer and must be purchased using money. Consequently, \(r^{(1)*}\) need not equal the stationary interest rate. It represents an initial transition condition, whereas from period 2 onward capital is accumulated internally by the firm and the stationary recursion applies.

section: Steady State: A \(4\times2\) Equality-Form Wide-Sense Structural Equilibrium Model
text:
Steady State: A \(4\times2\) Equality-Form Wide-Sense Structural Equilibrium Model
The steady state can be represented by a finite-dimensional equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model.
Assume the following:

There are four commodity types: product, labor, money, and an equity claim; and two economic-agent types: firm and consumer. Product is the numeraire. The equity claim represents the return on internally accumulated capital.
The consumer supplies \(\omega>0\) units of labor, one unit of money, and one unit of the equity claim, and consumes only product.
The production function is

\[
y=\alpha k^\theta l^{1-\theta},
\qquad
\alpha>0,
\qquad
0<\theta<1
\]

Let \(\rho\in(0,1)\) denote the exogenous intertemporal discount factor. The steady-state money interest rate and equity return rate are exogenously given by

\[
r_m=r_e=\frac1{\rho}-1
\]
Let
\[
\mathbf p=(1,p_l,p_m,p_e)^\top
\]
where \(p_l\), \(p_m\), and \(p_e\) are the prices of labor, money, and the equity claim, respectively. The prices of money and equity represent the interest on a unit of money and the dividend on a unit of equity, respectively. Because \(r_m=r_e\), the common factor \(1+r_m=1+r_e\) does not affect the firm’s optimal capital-labor ratio. For a given output level \(y\), its capital and labor demands are therefore
\[
k
=
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\theta p_l}{1-\theta}
\right)^{1-\theta}
\]
and
\[
l
=
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{1-\theta}{\theta p_l}
\right)^\theta
\]
Capital is carried internally and therefore does not require money. Labor purchases require money, while the return on internally accumulated capital is transferred through the equity claim. Accordingly, the demand and supply matrices are
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\theta p_l}{1-\theta}
\right)^{1-\theta}
&
c
\\[10pt]
\displaystyle
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{1-\theta}{\theta p_l}
\right)^\theta
&
0
\\[10pt]
\displaystyle
\frac{r_mp_l}{p_m}
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{1-\theta}{\theta p_l}
\right)^\theta
&
\displaystyle
\frac{r_mc}{p_m}
\\[12pt]
\displaystyle
\frac{r_e}{p_e}
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\theta p_l}{1-\theta}
\right)^{1-\theta}
&
0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf S(y)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y&0\\
0&\omega\\
0&1\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
where the first and second columns correspond to the firm and consumer, respectively.
The steady-state equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model is
\[
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)
=
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf S(y)
\]
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)\mathbf 1
=
\mathbf S(y)\mathbf 1
\]
Solving the model gives
\[
k^*=\theta\rho y^*,
\qquad
l^*=\omega,
\qquad
c^*=(1-\theta\rho)y^*
\]
and
\[
y^*
=
\alpha^{\frac1{1-\theta}}
(\theta\rho)^{\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}}
\omega
\]
Hence,
\[
k^*
=
(\theta\rho\alpha)^{\frac1{1-\theta}}\omega
\]
and
\[
c^*
=
(1-\theta\rho)
\alpha^{\frac1{1-\theta}}
(\theta\rho)^{\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}}
\omega
\]
The equilibrium prices are
\[
p_l^*
=
\rho(1-\theta)\frac{y^*}{\omega}
\]
\[
p_e^*
=
r_e k^*
=
\theta(1-\rho)y^*
\]
and
\[
p_m^*
=
r_m
\left(
p_l^*\omega+c^*
\right)
=
\frac{1-\rho}{\rho}
\left(
1+\rho-2\theta\rho
\right)y^*
\]
The corresponding money holdings are
\[
h_f^*
=
\frac{\rho(1-\theta)}
{1+\rho-2\theta\rho},
\qquad
h_c^*
=
\frac{1-\theta\rho}
{1+\rho-2\theta\rho}
\]
and the equilibrium demand for the equity claim is
\[
e^*=1
\]
